Animals smaller than a house cat.Mouse: A house mouse weighs about 20 grams. Mice can squeeze through a gap about the width of a pencil.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Hamster: A Syrian hamster weighs around 150 grams, a small fraction of a house cat. Its cheek pouches can stretch back to its hips.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Hummingbird: The bee hummingbird weighs about 2 grams and is the smallest bird. Its heart beats over 1,000 times a minute.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Shrew: The Etruscan shrew weighs about 2 grams and is the smallest mammal by mass. It eats about twice its weight daily.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Gerbil: A small desert rodent, only about 50 to 100 grams. Gerbils thump their hind legs to warn each other.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Chipmunk: A small ground squirrel weighing about 100 grams. It can carry large amounts of food in its cheek pouches.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Sparrow: A sparrow weighs roughly 25 to 40 grams. It is one of the most widespread wild birds, living alongside people.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Gecko: Many geckos are only a few centimetres long. Some can drop their tails to escape predators and later regrow them.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Canary: A small songbird of about 20 grams. Miners once used canaries as early warnings for dangerous gases.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Goldfish: A goldfish can live 10 to 20 years, and the oldest was said to have lived over 40. It's far smaller than a cat.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Ladybug: A ladybug is under a centimetre, tiny and light. It can eat many aphids in a day.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Mole: A small mammal of about 100 grams that lives underground. Its velvety fur lies in any direction, so it can move backward without trouble.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Raccoon: A raccoon weighs about 5 to 10 kilograms, usually heavier than a typical house cat of about 4 kilograms.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Beaver: A beaver weighs about 15 to 30 kilograms, far heavier than a house cat. Its incisors keep growing and have orange enamel.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Badger: A European badger weighs about 10 to 12 kilograms, much heavier than a cat. It lives in underground setts.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Otter: Even the smaller river otters weigh around 5 to 10 kilograms, so heavier than a house cat.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Wolf: A wolf weighs 30 to 50 kilograms, many times a cat. Wolf packs usually are a family, with parents and their young.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Goat: A goat weighs far more than a cat, often 50 kilograms or more. Goats were domesticated about 10,000 years ago.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Kangaroo: A red kangaroo can weigh 90 kilograms, far more than a cat. A kangaroo can't walk backward easily.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Swan: A swan can weigh about 10 kilograms, so well over a house cat. Swans can fly at high altitudes.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Turkey: A wild turkey can weigh over 8 kilograms, heavier than a house cat. Wild turkeys can fly short distances, up to about 90 km/h.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Deer: A white-tailed deer weighs around 60 to 100 kilograms. It's much heavier than a cat.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Sheep: A sheep weighs 45 to 160 kilograms, far more than a cat. Sheep have excellent memories for faces, including other sheep.
Animals smaller than a house cat.Pig: A pig can weigh from 100 to over 300 kilograms, many times a house cat. Pigs are among the smartest farm animals.

Animals that eat mostly insects.Anteater: Giant anteaters can eat up to about 30,000 ants and termites a day. They have no teeth and rely on a sticky tongue up to 60 cm long.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Aardvark: Aardvark means 'earth pig' in Afrikaans, but it's closer to elephants than pigs. At night it digs into termite mounds with powerful claws.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Pangolin: Pangolins have no teeth, so they swallow small stones to help grind ants and termites in their stomach. They're the only mammals covered in scales.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Numbat: The numbat is an Australian marsupial that is active in daytime, unusual for its kind. It can eat up to about 20,000 termites a day.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Echidna: The echidna uses a snout-like beak and sticky tongue to eat ants and termites. It has no teeth, mashing food against its palate.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Shrew: Shrews have such a fast metabolism that many must eat every few hours. Beyond insects, they eat worms and snails.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Hedgehog: A hedgehog eats beetles, caterpillars, worms and slugs. Despite old pictures of it carrying apples, fruit is not its choice food.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Swift: Swifts catch and eat insects in flight, and can stay airborne for months without landing. They even sleep while flying.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Swallow: Swallows scoop up flies and other insects mid-air as they swoop. They migrate thousands of kilometres between continents each year.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Chameleon: A chameleon's tongue can launch out at over 20 body-lengths per second to snag insects. Each eye also moves on its own.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Aardwolf: The aardwolf is a hyena relative that eats almost nothing but termites. It may swallow up to 200,000 in a single night.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Gecko: Geckos eat crickets, moths and other insects. Millions of microscopic hairs on their toes let them cling to glass.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Koala: Koalas eat almost only eucalyptus leaves, which are toxic to most animals. They sleep up to 20 hours a day to digest it.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Panda: Pandas are bears that eat mostly bamboo, up to about 12 kg a day. Their wrist bone works as a thumb for gripping stalks.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Spotted hyena: Spotted hyenas are strong hunters and scavengers. Their jaws can crunch through bone, and they digest it for the calcium.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Giraffe: Giraffes browse acacia leaves, using a long, dark tongue. Their necks have the same seven vertebrae as ours, only far longer.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Manatee: Manatees graze on seagrass and other aquatic plants. They can eat roughly a tenth of their body weight daily.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Beaver: Beavers eat bark, twigs and aquatic plants, not wood chips. Their specialised gut bacteria let them digest cellulose.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Rabbit: Rabbits are strictly herbivores and re-eat special soft droppings to extract more nutrients. Their teeth never stop growing.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Lion: Lions are hypercarnivores that mostly hunt zebra, wildebeest and buffalo. They sleep up to about 20 hours a day.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Shark: Sharks mostly eat fish, seals and squid, not insects. Whale sharks, the biggest of them, strain tiny plankton.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Parrot: Parrots eat seeds, fruit and nuts, so are no insect specialists. Some New Zealand kea, however, will tear into sheep fat for food.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Iguana: Adult iguanas are largely leaf-eating herbivores. Juveniles do eat insects, but they switch to plants as they age.
Animals that eat mostly insects.Tortoise: Tortoises are mostly grazers on grasses, weeds and flowers. Some, like the Galápagos giant, can live for well over a century.

Japanese ingredients.Miso: Miso is fermented soybean paste, and Japanese cooks often say a good miso soup is the heart of a meal; darker ones are aged longer.
Japanese ingredients.Nori: Nori is dried seaweed pressed into sheets like paper, and it's the black wrapper on sushi rolls and onigiri.
Japanese ingredients.Wasabi: Real wasabi is a rhizome that's hard to farm; most 'wasabi' paste in restaurants is just horseradish dyed green.
Japanese ingredients.Dashi: Dashi is the broth of kombu and bonito flakes, and it supplies the savory depth known as umami, first isolated in Japan.
Japanese ingredients.Mirin: Mirin is a sweet rice wine used in glazes, and it adds both sugar and shine to dishes like teriyaki.
Japanese ingredients.Edamame: Edamame are young soybeans in the pod, picked before they harden, and they're usually boiled and salted.
Japanese ingredients.Panko: Panko are Japanese breadcrumbs made from crustless bread, coarser and lighter than Western crumbs, so they fry up extra crisp.
Japanese ingredients.Matcha: Matcha is stone-ground powder of shade-grown green tea leaves, and you drink the whole leaf, not just the infusion.
Japanese ingredients.Umeboshi: Umeboshi are pickled ume, a fruit related to apricots, and are so sour and salty that they're eaten in tiny bits with rice.
Japanese ingredients.Natto: Natto is sticky fermented soybeans with a strong smell and stringy texture, and it's a common breakfast in Japan.
Japanese ingredients.Shiso: Shiso is a leaf of the mint family, with a minty, citrus-like flavor, often served with sashimi; the red and green varieties differ in taste.
Japanese ingredients.Kombu: Kombu is thick kelp that gives dashi its depth, and it's one of the richest natural sources of glutamate.
Japanese ingredients.Kimchi: Kimchi is Korean, spicy fermented cabbage, and there are hundreds of varieties; Japan has its own pickles but not this one.
Japanese ingredients.Gochujang: Gochujang is a fermented Korean red chili paste, with sweet and savory notes, so it's not Japanese.
Japanese ingredients.Hoisin: Hoisin is a sweet-savory Chinese sauce, so it's not Japanese, and the name literally means 'seafood' in Cantonese though it contains none.
Japanese ingredients.Paneer: Paneer is a fresh Indian cheese that doesn't melt, and so it's a South Asian staple rather than a Japanese one.
Japanese ingredients.Tahini: Tahini is sesame paste from the Middle East, and it's the key ingredient in hummus, not a Japanese ingredient.
Japanese ingredients.Sriracha: Sriracha is a Thai hot sauce named for Si Racha, so it's from Thailand, not Japan.
Japanese ingredients.Fish sauce: Fish sauce is a Southeast Asian staple of fermented anchovies and salt, and Roman garum was similar, but it isn't a Japanese ingredient.
Japanese ingredients.Harissa: Harissa is a North African chili paste from Tunisia, which is not a Japanese ingredient.
Japanese ingredients.Ghee: Ghee is clarified butter from India, simmered until the milk solids are removed, and it isn't Japanese.
Japanese ingredients.Doenjang: Doenjang is a Korean fermented soybean paste, similar to miso but stronger, so it belongs to Korean cuisine.
Japanese ingredients.Sambal: Sambal is a chili paste from Indonesia and Malaysia, with countless regional varieties, so it's not Japanese.
Japanese ingredients.Tamarind: Tamarind is a tangy pod pulp used in India and Southeast Asia, and the tree comes from Africa, so it's not Japanese.

Classic dim sum.Har gow: Har gow are translucent shrimp dumplings, and a good chef's wrapper should have at least seven pleats, a classic test of skill.
Classic dim sum.Siu mai: Siu mai are open-topped pork and shrimp dumplings, often crowned with a dot of orange roe or a pea.
Classic dim sum.Char siu bao: Char siu bao are fluffy steamed buns filled with sweet barbecued pork, and the baked version has a glazed golden top.
Classic dim sum.Cheung fun: Cheung fun are silky rice noodle rolls, made by steaming a thin batter, and typically served with sweet soy sauce.
Classic dim sum.Egg tart: The Hong Kong egg tart owes its custard filling to British influence, and its flaky pastry is a colonial legacy.
Classic dim sum.Turnip cake: Turnip cake is actually made from daikon radish, steamed, then pan-fried until crisp, and often includes bits of sausage.
Classic dim sum.Lotus leaf rice: Lotus leaf rice is sticky rice with chicken or pork steamed in a lotus leaf, which gives the dish a subtle tea-like fragrance.
Classic dim sum.Custard bun: The custard bun, or nai wong bao, is filled with a creamy, sweet salted egg yolk custard that may ooze when torn.
Classic dim sum.Sesame balls: Sesame balls are deep-fried glutinous rice dough covered in seeds; they puff up hollow, with a sweet red bean or lotus paste center.
Classic dim sum.Chicken feet: Chicken feet are braised until the skin turns tender and gelatinous; they are a famous dim sum item, loved for the collagen-rich bite.
Classic dim sum.Ramen: Ramen is a Japanese noodle soup of Chinese origin, and so it isn't a dim sum dish.
Classic dim sum.Sushi: Sushi is Japanese, not Cantonese, so it doesn't appear on a dim sum cart.
Classic dim sum.Pad thai: Pad thai is a Thai stir-fried noodle dish that was promoted in the 1930s and 40s as a national dish.
Classic dim sum.Bibimbap: Bibimbap is Korean, a rice bowl of vegetables and a fried egg, and the name means 'mixed rice'.
Classic dim sum.Pho: Pho is a Vietnamese beef noodle soup, and it's not a Cantonese dim sum item.
Classic dim sum.Tempura: Tempura is Japanese battered, fried food, likely brought by Portuguese traders, and isn't dim sum.
Classic dim sum.Kimchi: Kimchi is Korean fermented vegetables, so it isn't part of the Cantonese dim sum tradition.
Classic dim sum.Takoyaki: Takoyaki are octopus balls from Osaka in Japan, so they are not dim sum.
Classic dim sum.Satay: Satay are skewers of grilled meat from Indonesia and Malaysia, served with peanut sauce, and aren't dim sum.
Classic dim sum.Fortune cookie: Fortune cookies are a Japanese-American and Californian invention, not served in China, so they don't belong in a dim sum cart.
Classic dim sum.Mochi: Mochi are Japanese rice cakes pounded from glutinous rice, so they differ from Chinese dim sum desserts.
Classic dim sum.Banh mi: Banh mi is a Vietnamese baguette sandwich, a legacy of French colonial rule, and not dim sum.
Classic dim sum.Bulgogi: Bulgogi is Korean marinated beef, grilled, whose name means 'fire meat'.
Classic dim sum.Onigiri: Onigiri are Japanese rice balls, a popular snack in Japan, so they aren't dim sum.

Cities in China.Beijing: Beijing's Forbidden City held 24 emperors across the Ming and Qing dynasties, and has nearly 1,000 buildings.
Cities in China.Shanghai: Shanghai has the world's busiest container port, and its maglev train reaches about 430 km/h.
Cities in China.Guangzhou: Guangzhou was once known to the West as Canton, and it's the heart of Cantonese cuisine, including dim sum.
Cities in China.Shenzhen: Shenzhen grew from a fishing town into a city of over 17 million in about forty years, and is a center for electronics.
Cities in China.Chengdu: Chengdu is the home of giant pandas, with a research base to breed them, and of spicy Sichuan cuisine.
Cities in China.Wuhan: Wuhan sits on the Yangtze, and it was where the 1911 uprising that ended imperial rule began.
Cities in China.Xi'an: Xi'an is where the Terracotta Army was found in 1974, thousands of clay soldiers buried with the first emperor.
Cities in China.Nanjing: Nanjing's name means southern capital, and it served as capital of China at several points, most recently in the 1920s and 30s.
Cities in China.Hangzhou: Hangzhou's West Lake has been praised by poets for centuries, and it's home to Alibaba.
Cities in China.Chongqing: Chongqing is a mountain city with hot pot as its signature dish, and it has trains running through apartment buildings.
Cities in China.Harbin: Harbin hosts a huge winter festival of ice sculptures, and temperatures there can fall below minus 30 Celsius.
Cities in China.Tokyo: Tokyo is Japan's capital, and Japanese kanji characters were borrowed from Chinese, which is why the two look so alike on signs.
Cities in China.Seoul: Seoul is the capital of South Korea, and has been a capital for over 600 years.
Cities in China.Hanoi: Hanoi is Vietnam's capital, founded as Thang Long in 1010, and its Old Quarter streets are named for the goods once sold there.
Cities in China.Ulaanbaatar: Ulaanbaatar is the capital of Mongolia, and is one of the coldest capital cities in the world.
Cities in China.Bangkok: Bangkok is the capital of Thailand, and a city of canals once called the Venice of the East.
Cities in China.Singapore: Singapore is a city-state, and it has a majority ethnically Chinese population, but it's an independent country.
Cities in China.Busan: Busan is South Korea's second-largest city and its main port.
Cities in China.Osaka: Osaka is in Japan, and its castle was built by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who unified the country.
Cities in China.Kyoto: Kyoto is in Japan, and was modeled on the Tang dynasty capital of Chang'an, which is today's Xi'an.
Cities in China.Manila: Manila is in the Philippines, and has one of the world's oldest Chinatowns, Binondo.
Cities in China.Kuala Lumpur: Kuala Lumpur is the capital of Malaysia, home of the Petronas Towers, once the tallest buildings in the world.
Cities in China.Yangon: Yangon is Myanmar's largest city, and has the golden Shwedagon Pagoda.
Cities in China.Vientiane: Vientiane is Laos's capital, a small riverside city on the Mekong, across from Thailand.

States the Mississippi River touches.Minnesota: The river begins here as a stream small enough to wade across at Lake Itasca, then runs about 2,300 miles to the Gulf.
States the Mississippi River touches.Wisconsin: Its western border follows the river, where bluffs and backwaters make up the Driftless Area that glaciers skipped.
States the Mississippi River touches.Iowa: The river forms the entire eastern border, and its steamboat-era towns like Dubuque and Davenport still sit on the bluffs.
States the Mississippi River touches.Illinois: The Mississippi bounds the west side, and it meets the Ohio River at Cairo, the state's southern tip.
States the Mississippi River touches.Missouri: St. Louis' Gateway Arch stands on the river's west bank, and the muddy Missouri River joins it just north of the city.
States the Mississippi River touches.Kentucky: Its far western tip touches the river, a small slice that surprises people who think of the state as only the Ohio River's neighbor.
States the Mississippi River touches.Tennessee: Memphis sits on bluffs above the river, and the state's western border is defined by it.
States the Mississippi River touches.Arkansas: The river runs along the eastern border, bordering the fertile Delta region of cotton and rice.
States the Mississippi River touches.Mississippi: The state is named for the river, and its Delta region is the legendary birthplace of blues music.
States the Mississippi River touches.Louisiana: The river ends here, in a delta that is steadily sinking, passing New Orleans before reaching the Gulf.
States the Mississippi River touches.Ohio: Trap: the Ohio River is the one on its border, but the Mississippi itself is far to the west.
States the Mississippi River touches.Indiana: Trap: the Wabash and Ohio rivers define its edges, while the Mississippi flows through states to the west.
States the Mississippi River touches.Alabama: Trap: its biggest river, the Tombigbee, flows to Mobile Bay, so the Mississippi never touches it.
States the Mississippi River touches.Kansas: Trap: the Missouri River borders its northeast corner, but the Mississippi itself is a state or two farther east.
States the Mississippi River touches.Nebraska: Trap: the Platte and Missouri rivers shape it, but the Mississippi is hundreds of miles east.
States the Mississippi River touches.Oklahoma: Trap: the Red and Arkansas rivers cross it, and both eventually feed the Mississippi without it touching the state.
States the Mississippi River touches.Texas: Trap: despite its size, none of its borders touch the Mississippi, and the Sabine and Red rivers are what it shares.
States the Mississippi River touches.Michigan: Trap: surrounded by Great Lakes, it has no Mississippi frontage.
States the Mississippi River touches.Georgia: Trap: its rivers flow to the Atlantic or the Gulf directly, not into the Mississippi.
States the Mississippi River touches.Colorado: Trap: though the Rockies feed rivers like the Arkansas, which join the Mississippi, the river itself never reaches this state.
States the Mississippi River touches.North Dakota: Trap: the Missouri River crosses it and ends up at the Mississippi, but only far downstream.
States the Mississippi River touches.South Dakota: Trap: the Missouri River splits the state in two and reaches the Mississippi near St. Louis, well away from the border.
States the Mississippi River touches.Montana: Trap: the Missouri River begins here, which is technically the longest branch of the Mississippi system, but the Mississippi itself is not in Montana.
States the Mississippi River touches.Florida: Trap: its rivers drain to the Atlantic and the Gulf of Mexico directly, not through the Mississippi.

Places in Norway.Oslo: Norway's capital hosts the Nobel Peace Prize ceremony each December, the only Nobel awarded outside Sweden.
Places in Norway.Bergen: The rainy gateway to the fjords, with colorful Bryggen wharf houses, is said to see rain on over 200 days a year.
Places in Norway.Tromsø: Sitting well above the Arctic Circle, it is a prime spot for aurora viewing, with the sun not rising for weeks in winter.
Places in Norway.Lofoten: An Arctic archipelago of jagged peaks and fishing villages, famous for its dried cod, stockfish, hung on wooden racks.
Places in Norway.Geirangerfjord: A narrow UNESCO fjord framed by waterfalls like the Seven Sisters, carved by glaciers into steep cliffs.
Places in Norway.Stavanger: Norway's oil capital, with a well-preserved old town of white wooden houses and the fjord region nearby.
Places in Norway.Trondheim: Medieval capital of Norway, home to Nidaros Cathedral, northern Europe's largest medieval building, where kings are blessed.
Places in Norway.Svalbard: This Arctic archipelago has a global seed vault, polar bears outnumbering residents in some counts, and no visa requirement for anyone.
Places in Norway.Pulpit Rock: Preikestolen is a flat cliff top about 600 meters above the Lysefjord with no railing.
Places in Norway.Ålesund: Rebuilt in Art Nouveau style after a fire in 1904, with towers and spires set among islands.
Places in Norway.North Cape: A cliff at the top of Europe, widely regarded as the northernmost point reachable by road on the continent, at around 71 degrees north.
Places in Norway.Lillehammer: Host city of the 1994 Winter Olympics, with an open-air museum of old farm buildings.
Places in Norway.Stockholm: Sweden's capital, built on 14 islands, and home of the Nobel Prize banquet.
Places in Norway.Gothenburg: Sweden's second city, a port on the west coast, known for the Volvo carmaker founded there in 1927.
Places in Norway.Malmö: A Swedish city joined to Copenhagen by the Oresund Bridge, which became a Scandi noir TV hit.
Places in Norway.Helsinki: Finland's capital, a Baltic port with a rock church carved into granite and a strong design tradition.
Places in Norway.Copenhagen: Denmark's capital is the home of Tivoli Gardens, one of the world's oldest amusement parks, opened in 1843.
Places in Norway.Reykjavik: Iceland's capital, the world's northernmost capital of a sovereign state, heated largely by geothermal energy.
Places in Norway.Tórshavn: The capital of the Faroe Islands, one of the smallest capitals in the world, with a turf-roofed old town.
Places in Norway.Rovaniemi: This Finnish Lapland city claims to be Santa Claus's official hometown, sitting on the Arctic Circle.
Places in Norway.Kiruna: Sweden's northernmost town, where an enormous iron ore mine is so vast that the town is being relocated.
Places in Norway.Uppsala: Home to Sweden's oldest university, founded in 1477, and the tomb of Linnaeus, the father of taxonomy.
Places in Norway.Aarhus: A Danish city that was the European Capital of Culture in 2017, with a famous rainbow panorama on a museum roof.
Places in Norway.Nuuk: The capital of Greenland, one of the smallest capitals in the world, and nearer to Canada than to Norway.

Flightless birds.Ostrich: The largest living bird, standing up to about 2.7 meters. It can sprint at around 70 km/h, and its eye is bigger than its brain.
Flightless birds.Emu: Australia's tallest bird, which can run about 50 km/h. The male sits on the eggs for about eight weeks, barely eating.
Flightless birds.Penguin: Its wings became flippers that swim underwater, fast. Emperor penguins can dive deeper than 500 meters.
Flightless birds.Kiwi: New Zealand's national bird lays an enormous egg, about a fifth of its body weight. Its nostrils sit at the tip of its beak to sniff out worms.
Flightless birds.Cassowary: A big, helmeted bird of New Guinea and northern Australia, with dagger-like claws. It is sometimes called the world's most dangerous bird.
Flightless birds.Rhea: South America's largest bird, an ostrich lookalike. Males gather eggs from several females and raise the chicks alone.
Flightless birds.Kakapo: A rare nocturnal parrot of New Zealand, the heaviest in the world. Fewer than 300 are alive, and each is named and monitored.
Flightless birds.Dodo: Lived only on Mauritius and was extinct within about a century of human arrival, in the 1600s. It's now a symbol of extinction.
Flightless birds.Great auk: A penguin-like bird of the North Atlantic, hunted to extinction by 1844. The original penguin was this bird, and the name later moved to Antarctic birds.
Flightless birds.Peacock: A trap: it flies, though poorly. Its famous train is shed and regrown each year.
Flightless birds.Puffin: A trap: it flies, flapping its wings up to 400 times per minute. It also swims underwater with them.
Flightless birds.Albatross: A trap: it flies superbly, with a wingspan up to about 3.5 meters. It can glide for hours without flapping.
Flightless birds.Hummingbird: A trap: it flies, and can hover and even fly backward, beating its wings up to about 80 times per second.
Flightless birds.Pelican: A trap: it flies well despite its size. Its beak pouch can hold more than its belly can.
Flightless birds.Flamingo: A trap: it flies. Its pink color comes from pigments in the shrimp and algae it eats.
Flightless birds.Swan: A trap: a swan flies, strongly, and mute swans are among the heaviest flying birds.
Flightless birds.Roadrunner: A trap: it can fly but prefers running, at about 30 km/h, and feeds on snakes and lizards.
Flightless birds.Kookaburra: A trap: a kingfisher famous for its laughing call, but it flies perfectly well, and swoops down on lizards and snakes.
Flightless birds.Toucan: A trap: it flies, though not far. Its huge beak is light and hollow, and it helps the bird shed body heat.
Flightless birds.Owl: A trap: owls fly in near silence thanks to feathers with soft, fringed edges, which help them ambush prey.
Flightless birds.Vulture: A trap: vultures fly, soaring on rising warm air for hours without flapping, scanning for carcasses from high up.
Flightless birds.Heron: A trap: it flies strongly, folding its neck into an S shape in flight, which distinguishes it from cranes, which fly with necks outstretched.
Flightless birds.Seagull: A trap: gulls are strong fliers, and will drop shellfish onto hard ground from the air to crack them open.
Flightless birds.Parrot: A trap: nearly all parrots fly well. The kakapo is the unusual exception, which makes it a famous flightless parrot.

Grasses (botanically).Wheat: A grass, and the world's most widely grown crop by area. Its grains are the seeds of the plant and the basis of bread.
Grasses (botanically).Rice: A semi-aquatic grass that feeds roughly half the planet. It was domesticated in the Yangtze valley more than 8,000 years ago.
Grasses (botanically).Corn: Corn is a giant grass, domesticated from a wild plant called teosinte, which bore only a handful of hard kernels per ear.
Grasses (botanically).Oats: A grass grown for its seeds. Oats were once considered a weed in wheat fields before people noticed they were worth growing.
Grasses (botanically).Barley: One of the first domesticated grains, and the main source of malt for beer and whisky. It's also a grass.
Grasses (botanically).Rye: A hardy grass that thrives in poor, cold soils where wheat fails. It's the main grain in pumpernickel bread.
Grasses (botanically).Bamboo: The giant of the grass family, and some species grow nearly a meter in a day. Flowering happens only once every several decades for many types.
Grasses (botanically).Sugarcane: A tall tropical grass whose stalks are rich in sugar. It supplies most of the world's sugar and the ethanol fuel burned in Brazil.
Grasses (botanically).Lemongrass: A real grass, with a citrusy aroma from citral, the same compound found in lemon peel. It's a staple of Thai cooking.
Grasses (botanically).Pampas grass: Native to South America, this giant grass sports plumes up to a few meters tall. It's grown as an ornamental but invasive in places.
Grasses (botanically).Millet: A group of small-seeded grasses that have been eaten in Africa and Asia for thousands of years. They're very drought-tolerant.
Grasses (botanically).Sorghum: A grass that thrives in heat and drought, and a staple across Africa. It's also used to make syrup, brooms and biofuel.
Grasses (botanically).Wild rice: A grass that grows in shallow water in North America. It isn't closely related to ordinary rice, but its seeds are eaten much the same way.
Grasses (botanically).Quinoa: Not a grass at all, but a relative of spinach and beets. People treat it as a grain, which is why it's called a pseudocereal.
Grasses (botanically).Buckwheat: Despite its name, it isn't a wheat or even a grass. It's related to rhubarb and sorrel, which is why it's naturally gluten-free.
Grasses (botanically).Amaranth: A broadleaf plant grown for tiny seeds, not a grass. The Aztecs used it heavily, in food and in ritual.
Grasses (botanically).Chia: A member of the mint family, not a grass. Its seeds form a gel when soaked, which makes them popular in puddings.
Grasses (botanically).Flax: A broadleaf plant, grown for fiber and seeds. Linen is made from its stems, and linseed oil from its seeds.
Grasses (botanically).Clover: A legume, with three-part leaves rather than the narrow blades of grasses. It enriches the soil with nitrogen.
Grasses (botanically).Papyrus: A sedge, not a true grass, though it looks grassy. Egyptians made writing sheets from its stems, giving us the word paper.
Grasses (botanically).Scallion: A member of the onion family, not a grass, though its hollow green leaves look like blades. It's also known as the green onion.
Grasses (botanically).Moss: Mosses are tiny non-flowering plants with no true roots. Despite growing like a green carpet, they aren't grasses.
Grasses (botanically).Spinach: A leafy broadleaf plant in the amaranth family, far from grasses. The old tale of its super iron content stems from a misplaced decimal.
Grasses (botanically).Seaweed: Seaweeds are algae, not plants at all, so they can't be grasses. Seagrass, however, is a true flowering plant.

Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Goat: Goats' horns are never shed and keep growing through life, and they are made of bone covered with keratin.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Bull: A bull's horns are bone cores sheathed in keratin and are never shed, unlike antlers, so a bull does qualify.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Ram: A ram's curled horns keep growing for life, and can weigh a lot, and they clash in head-on fights.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Bison: Bison have short, curved horns on both sexes that are never shed. A full-grown bull weighs up to a ton.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Water buffalo: Water buffalo have broad sweeping horns that can span about two meters in some wild ones.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Antelope: Antelopes, from tiny dik-diks to giant elands, carry unbranched, permanent horns, many of them spiral.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Gazelle: Gazelles carry slender, ringed horns on both sexes, and they can sprint at over 60 miles per hour.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Ibex: Ibex have enormous backward-sweeping horns, with yearly growth rings you can count to tell age.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Yak: Yaks have wide-spreading horns, and they live at altitudes above 4,000 meters, in cold Himalayan areas.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Wildebeest: A wildebeest has hooked horns on both sexes, and migrates in the millions across the Serengeti.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Musk ox: Musk ox have horns that join into a helmet-like boss, and their coat is among the warmest of any animal's.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Deer: Deer grow antlers of solid bone, and they are shed and regrown yearly. That is why they are not horns.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Moose: Moose have the largest antlers of all deer, and they shed them each winter, so they are antlers, not horns.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Elk: Elk wear branching antlers of bone that are shed and regrown yearly, so they do not count as horns.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Reindeer: Reindeer are the only deer in which both sexes grow antlers, shed every year, and not horns.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Narwhal: A narwhal's spiral tusk is a very long tooth, up to about 2.5 meters, so it is a tusk and not a horn.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Elephant: Elephants have tusks, which are elongated teeth of ivory, so they are neither horns nor antlers.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Walrus: Walruses have tusks, which are long canine teeth, and they use them to haul themselves onto ice.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Warthog: A warthog's curved tusks are overgrown teeth, not horns, and it kneels on its wrists to feed.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Unicorn: The unicorn is mythical, and its single spiral horn is the kind of thing that only exists in stories.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Horse: Horses have no horns or antlers, and nothing grows on their heads, but they have one of the largest eyes of any land mammal.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Hippo: Hippos have huge tusk-like canine teeth, and no horns, and they can open their jaws nearly 180 degrees.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Llama: Llamas have no horns, though they are famous for spitting when annoyed. They are camelids, relatives of camels.
Animals with horns (not antlers or tusks.Camel: Camels have no horns, and their humps store fat, not water, so they can go long stretches without food.

X-Men characters.Wolverine: Logan's adamantium-laced skeleton and claws made him the breakout star, and Hugh Jackman played him in nine films between 2000 and 2017.
X-Men characters.Storm: Ororo Munroe controls weather, and she was a worshiped goddess in Africa before joining the X-Men.
X-Men characters.Cyclops: Scott Summers fires powerful optic beams, and his ruby-quartz visor is needed to keep them under control.
X-Men characters.Jean Grey: Jean is the telekinetic who becomes the cosmic Phoenix, and her death in the 'Dark Phoenix Saga' is one of comics' most famous stories.
X-Men characters.Professor X: Charles Xavier is the telepath who founded the school for gifted youngsters, and he is a rare wheelchair-using superhero.
X-Men characters.Magneto: Erik Lehnsherr, a Holocaust survivor who controls metal, is the X-Men's greatest enemy but often an ally.
X-Men characters.Rogue: Anna Marie absorbs memories and powers by touch, so she can't touch anyone without risk.
X-Men characters.Beast: Hank McCoy is a brilliant scientist with a blue-furred form, one of the original five X-Men.
X-Men characters.Gambit: The Cajun thief Remy LeBeau charges objects with kinetic energy and throws playing cards that explode.
X-Men characters.Nightcrawler: Kurt Wagner is a blue teleporter who vanishes with a 'bamf', and who is a devout Catholic.
X-Men characters.Mystique: Raven Darkholme is a shapeshifter who is also the mother of Nightcrawler in the comics.
X-Men characters.Iceman: Bobby Drake is another of the original five X-Men, who can cover himself in ice.
X-Men characters.Jubilee: Jubilation Lee shoots plasma 'fireworks', and she joined the team in the 1980s as a mall-rat teenager.
X-Men characters.Colossus: Piotr Rasputin is a Russian farm boy who can turn his skin to organic steel.
X-Men characters.Hulk: The Hulk is a Marvel hero, but he's an Avenger, not an X-Man.
X-Men characters.Thor: Thor is the Norse god of thunder and a founding Avenger, not a mutant X-Man.
X-Men characters.Hawkeye: Hawkeye is an Avengers archer and a normal human, not a mutant.
X-Men characters.Vision: Vision is an android Avenger, not a mutant X-Man.
X-Men characters.Black Widow: Natasha Romanoff is an Avengers spy, not an X-Man.
X-Men characters.Falcon: Sam Wilson, the Falcon, is an Avenger and Captain America's successor, not an X-Man.
X-Men characters.Daredevil: Daredevil is the blind lawyer of Hell's Kitchen, a street-level hero, not an X-Man.
X-Men characters.Silver Surfer: The Silver Surfer is a cosmic herald who first appeared in the Fantastic Four, not the X-Men.
X-Men characters.Human Torch: Johnny Storm is a member of the Fantastic Four, not the X-Men.
X-Men characters.Star-Lord: Star-Lord is the leader of Guardians of the Galaxy, not an X-Man.

Films based on Stephen King books.1408: Based on a short story, this one has John Cusack trapped in a haunted hotel room. The number's digits add up to 13.
Films based on Stephen King books.The Shining: King has long disliked Kubrick's 1980 version, saying it lacked the book's slow descent of Jack Torrance into madness.
Films based on Stephen King books.It: The 2017 film became the highest-grossing horror movie ever at the time, with Pennywise reimagined by Bill Skarsgard.
Films based on Stephen King books.Carrie: King's first published novel; he reportedly threw the draft away, and his wife Tabitha fished it out of the trash and urged him to finish.
Films based on Stephen King books.Misery: Kathy Bates won the Best Actress Oscar as Annie Wilkes, the fan who holds a novelist captive. Her role is among horror's rare Oscar wins.
Films based on Stephen King books.Stand by Me: Adapted from King's novella The Body, it is no horror at all: four boys hike to see a corpse, in one of his most loved coming-of-age tales.
Films based on Stephen King books.The Green Mile: King first published this story as a six-part serial in 1996, one slim paperback installment at a time.
Films based on Stephen King books.Pet Sematary: King once called this his most frightening book and nearly left it unpublished in a drawer. He even wrote a cameo into the 1989 film.
Films based on Stephen King books.Cujo: The killer is a St. Bernard, and the story is mostly set in one stalled Ford Pinto. King says he barely remembers writing it, amid heavy drinking.
Films based on Stephen King books.Christine: John Carpenter directed this tale of a possessed 1958 Plymouth Fury. Several cars were used, and many were wrecked during filming.
Films based on Stephen King books.The Mist: Frank Darabont's film ends far bleaker than King's open-ended novella, and King has said he wished he had thought of that ending himself.
Films based on Stephen King books.Doctor Sleep: A sequel to The Shining that follows grown-up Danny Torrance. The film tries to honor both King's novel and Kubrick's film.
Films based on Stephen King books.Firestarter: An eight-year-old Drew Barrymore plays the girl who can ignite things with her mind, and King wrote the novel about a secret government experiment.
Films based on Stephen King books.Halloween: Not King: John Carpenter's 1978 slasher was an original script. Carpenter did later direct King's Christine, which is probably the confusion.
Films based on Stephen King books.Scream: Not King: Kevin Williamson wrote it, and Wes Craven directed it. It spoofs the slasher genre that King's era helped popularize.
Films based on Stephen King books.The Exorcist: Not King: it came from William Peter Blatty's 1971 novel, inspired by a real 1949 exorcism case reported in the press.
Films based on Stephen King books.Psycho: Not King: it comes from Robert Bloch's novel, loosely inspired by killer Ed Gein. Hitchcock reportedly bought up copies to protect the twist.
Films based on Stephen King books.Jaws: Not King: Peter Benchley wrote the novel, and Spielberg's mechanical shark nicknamed Bruce kept breaking down, forcing the film to hide it.
Films based on Stephen King books.Rosemary's Baby: Not King: Ira Levin wrote it, and Roman Polanski directed. Levin also wrote The Stepford Wives.
Films based on Stephen King books.Get Out: Not King: it was Jordan Peele's original screenplay, and it won him the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay.
Films based on Stephen King books.A Quiet Place: Not King: it was an original script by Bryan Woods, Scott Beck and John Krasinski, who also directed it and co-starred with Emily Blunt.
Films based on Stephen King books.The Sixth Sense: Not King: M. Night Shyamalan wrote and directed it. His famous twist has been spoiled in pop culture for decades.
Films based on Stephen King books.The Ring: Not King: it is a remake of Japan's Ringu, which was based on Koji Suzuki's novel. A cursed videotape drives the plot.
Films based on Stephen King books.Jurassic Park: Not King: Michael Crichton wrote the novel. King is a horror writer; Crichton was the sci-fi thriller master behind the dinosaur DNA story.

Animals famous for their songs.Nightingale: Males sing at night to attract mates, and Keats wrote a famous ode about one, and it is a symbol of beautiful song.
Animals famous for their songs.Canary: Wild canaries come from the Canary Islands, which were named for dogs, not the other way round, and miners once used them to detect gas.
Animals famous for their songs.Humpback whale: Males sing songs that can last up to 20 minutes, and groups learn new ones from each other across the ocean.
Animals famous for their songs.Blackbird: The Beatles wrote a song about one, and males are black while females are brown, a pattern that makes them easy to tell apart.
Animals famous for their songs.Robin: It sings year-round, even at night near streetlights, and the American robin is actually a thrush.
Animals famous for their songs.Gibbon: These apes live in mated pairs that sing duets, and each species has its own distinct song.
Animals famous for their songs.Lark: The skylark sings while hovering high, inspiring Vaughan Williams's The Lark Ascending.
Animals famous for their songs.Mockingbird: Its Latin name Mimus polyglottos means many-tongued mimic, and one can learn over 100 songs.
Animals famous for their songs.Thrush: The song thrush repeats phrases and smashes snails on stones, using them as anvils.
Animals famous for their songs.Wren: A tiny bird with a very loud song for its size, and it is Britain's most common breeding bird by some counts.
Animals famous for their songs.Snake: Snakes have no external ears, and they hiss, but they do not sing, sensing vibration through the ground.
Animals famous for their songs.Giraffe: A 2015 study found giraffes hum at night, but they are mostly silent and were once thought completely mute.
Animals famous for their songs.Jellyfish: No brain, no ears, no voice, and they drift in silence.
Animals famous for their songs.Turtle: Turtles are largely silent, with only rare calls, though some species coo to their eggs.
Animals famous for their songs.Rabbit: Rabbits are quiet, except for a scream of terror when seized by a predator.
Animals famous for their songs.Spider: Spiders may drum or vibrate, but they have no real song, and some males send courtship signals by vibration.
Animals famous for their songs.Worm: Worms are deaf and silent, though they feel vibrations in the soil.
Animals famous for their songs.Sloth: Sloths seldom make a sound, other than a baby's cry, and move so slowly that algae grows on their fur.
Animals famous for their songs.Octopus: Octopuses are silent, and they have three hearts and blue blood.
Animals famous for their songs.Crab: Fiddler crabs wave a single oversized claw, not sing, and that is how they attract mates.
Animals famous for their songs.Snail: Snails are silent, and some can sleep for years.
Animals famous for their songs.Starfish: Starfish have no voice at all, and no brain either.
Animals famous for their songs.Butterfly: Butterflies flutter silently, and they taste with their feet.
Animals famous for their songs.Goldfish: Goldfish can hear well, but they are silent, and they can live for decades.

Words for animal noises.Moo: Moo is the same in many languages; Hebrew speakers say 'mu' and Japanese 'moh', showing how similar cows sound to humans.
Words for animal noises.Oink: English pigs say oink, but Dutch pigs say 'knor' and Japanese ones 'buu buu', as each language hears them differently.
Words for animal noises.Woof: Dogs say woof in English, 'wan wan' in Japanese and 'guau' in Spanish, though the animal makes the same sound.
Words for animal noises.Meow: Meow is mostly a cat's way of talking to people; wild adult cats rarely use it with each other.
Words for animal noises.Neigh: A horse's neigh can carry a lot of information, like its identity and mood, to others in the herd.
Words for animal noises.Baa: Lambs and their mothers can pick out each other's baa among a whole flock, even in a noisy field.
Words for animal noises.Quack: The old myth that a duck's quack does not echo is false; it does echo, though it can be hard to notice.
Words for animal noises.Hiss: Cats and snakes hiss as a warning; the sound mimics the rush of air that signals 'back off'.
Words for animal noises.Roar: A lion's roar can be heard from about 8 kilometers away, which helps it mark territory across the savanna.
Words for animal noises.Cluck: Hens cluck to their chicks even before the eggs hatch, and chicks answer from inside the shell.
Words for animal noises.Bray: A donkey's bray can carry for several kilometers across open desert, which helps the animals keep in touch.
Words for animal noises.Hoot: Owls hoot to defend territory and find mates; each species has its own pattern, like a spoken name.
Words for animal noises.Ribbit: Only male frogs ribbit, and only some species do; the sound became famous partly through Hollywood films.
Words for animal noises.Chirp: Crickets chirp faster when it is warmer, and the rate can be used to roughly estimate the temperature.
Words for animal noises.Ding: Trap: ding is the sound of a bell or elevator, not of any animal.
Words for animal noises.Clang: Trap: clang imitates metal striking metal, like a bell or a pot, not an animal's call.
Words for animal noises.Beep: Trap: beep is a machine sound, from a horn or a device, and is not made by any animal.
Words for animal noises.Vroom: Trap: vroom imitates an engine revving, so it fits cars and motorbikes, not animals.
Words for animal noises.Tick: Trap: tick is a clock sound, though a tick is also a small creature, which makes it a sneaky animal word.
Words for animal noises.Boing: Trap: boing imitates a spring or a bouncy jump, not any animal's voice.
Words for animal noises.Splash: Trap: splash is an animal-adjacent sound, like a fish jumping, but it is a water noise, not an animal call.
Words for animal noises.Bang: Trap: bang is an explosion or a slam, not a sound an animal makes.
Words for animal noises.Clink: Trap: clink is the sound of glasses or coins touching, not an animal sound.
Words for animal noises.Choo-choo: Trap: choo-choo is how English imitates a steam train, with no animal involved.

Bands from Ireland.U2: U2 formed in Dublin in 1976 after Larry Mullen pinned a note on a school noticeboard seeking bandmates.
Bands from Ireland.The Cranberries: Limerick's Cranberries wrote Zombie in 1994, a protest song about the IRA bombing in Warrington, England.
Bands from Ireland.Thin Lizzy: Thin Lizzy, led by Dublin's Phil Lynott, rocked up the old Irish folk tune Whiskey in the Jar into a 1972 hit.
Bands from Ireland.The Corrs: The Corrs are three sisters and a brother from Dundalk, and they mixed pop with Irish folk instruments like the tin whistle.
Bands from Ireland.Westlife: Westlife, from Sligo, scored a record-matching run of UK number one singles, over a dozen of them.
Bands from Ireland.Boyzone: Boyzone was put together in Dublin in 1993 through auditions, with Ronan Keating as one of its lead voices.
Bands from Ireland.The Script: The Script formed in Dublin and found global fame with Danny O'Donoghue's powerful, emotional songs like Breakeven.
Bands from Ireland.Clannad: Clannad is a Donegal family band, and a young Enya was an early member before launching her own career.
Bands from Ireland.Kodaline: Kodaline, from Swords near Dublin, found fame with All I Want, a soaring ballad that featured in a TV drama.
Bands from Ireland.Oasis: Oasis come from Manchester, though the Gallagher brothers' parents were Irish, which is the trap here.
Bands from Ireland.The Beatles: The Beatles came from Liverpool, a port city with strong Irish links, but they are English.
Bands from Ireland.Coldplay: Coldplay formed in London in the late 1990s, so they're British, not Irish, despite many Irish-style anthems.
Bands from Ireland.Queen: Queen formed in London, with Freddie Mercury born in Zanzibar and Brian May and Roger Taylor English.
Bands from Ireland.Radiohead: Radiohead formed at school in Abingdon, Oxfordshire, so they are an English band.
Bands from Ireland.The Smiths: The Smiths came from Manchester, though Morrissey and Johnny Marr both have Irish parents.
Bands from Ireland.Travis: Travis formed in Glasgow, Scotland, and their song Why Does It Always Rain on Me? became a 1999 hit.
Bands from Ireland.Simple Minds: Simple Minds are from Glasgow, Scotland, and their 1985 hit Don't You (Forget About Me) headlined The Breakfast Club.
Bands from Ireland.Franz Ferdinand: Franz Ferdinand are Glaswegian and named after an archduke, whose 1914 assassination helped spark World War I.
Bands from Ireland.Arctic Monkeys: Arctic Monkeys formed in Sheffield, England, and their debut became the fastest-selling British debut album ever.
Bands from Ireland.Muse: Muse come from Teignmouth in Devon, England, and not from Ireland.
Bands from Ireland.Duran Duran: Keane formed in Battle, East Sussex, and made their piano-led sound without a guitarist.
Bands from Ireland.Keane: Duran Duran began in Birmingham, England, and took their name from a character in the film Barbarella.
Bands from Ireland.Blur: Blur formed in London in 1988 and came out of the Britpop rivalry with Oasis.
Bands from Ireland.Take That: Take That formed in Manchester in 1990, and the original lineup included Gary Barlow and Robbie Williams.

MLB team nicknames.Yankees: New York has won 27 World Series titles, the most in MLB; early on the team was called the Highlanders.
MLB team nicknames.Red Sox: Boston ended its 86-year title drought in 2004, a streak known as the 'Curse of the Bambino'.
MLB team nicknames.Dodgers: The name came from Brooklyn residents dodging trolley cars, and the team moved to Los Angeles in 1958.
MLB team nicknames.Cubs: Chicago won the 2016 World Series, ending a drought of 108 years, MLB's longest.
MLB team nicknames.Mets: Founded in 1962, the 'Miracle Mets' won the 1969 World Series with a team nobody expected to do so.
MLB team nicknames.Astros: Houston's name celebrates the city's space industry, and the team once played in the Astrodome, the first domed baseball stadium.
MLB team nicknames.Mariners: Seattle's name honors the city's maritime history; the team debuted in 1977.
MLB team nicknames.Orioles: Baltimore's name comes from the Maryland state bird, and Cal Ripken Jr. played a record 2,632 consecutive games for them.
MLB team nicknames.Padres: San Diego's name is Spanish for fathers, for the Franciscan friars who founded the city's mission.
MLB team nicknames.Phillies: Philadelphia has the most losses of any team in American pro sports, but won the World Series in 1980, 2008.
MLB team nicknames.Brewers: Milwaukee's name honors the city's beer-making tradition, and it began as the Seattle Pilots.
MLB team nicknames.Rockies: Colorado's team plays at high altitude in Denver, where balls fly farther, and the stadium stores balls in a humidor.
MLB team nicknames.Twins: Minnesota's name is for the Twin Cities of Minneapolis and St. Paul; the team started as the Washington Senators.
MLB team nicknames.Blue Jays: Toronto's team won the World Series in 1992 and 1993, the first non-US team to win it.
MLB team nicknames.Lakers: A Los Angeles NBA team, whose name came from Minnesota's lakes, so not a baseball team.
MLB team nicknames.Celtics: An NBA team from Boston, with 18 titles, and not a baseball club; Boston's baseball team is the Red Sox.
MLB team nicknames.Packers: A Wisconsin NFL team named for a meatpacking company, so a football name, not baseball.
MLB team nicknames.Patriots: New England's NFL team, which won six Super Bowls, so it's a football name, not baseball.
MLB team nicknames.Bruins: Boston's NHL team, which joined the league in 1924, and is not a baseball club.
MLB team nicknames.Canucks: Vancouver's NHL team, which has no MLB equivalent as Canada's only MLB side is the Blue Jays.
MLB team nicknames.Knicks: New York's NBA team, short for Knickerbockers, and not a baseball club like the Yankees or Mets.
MLB team nicknames.Steelers: Pittsburgh's NFL team, named for the city's steel industry; its baseball side is the Pirates.
MLB team nicknames.Seahawks: Seattle's NFL team, so it's football; the city's baseball side is the Mariners.
MLB team nicknames.Maple Leafs: Toronto's NHL team; the city's baseball club is the Blue Jays, so don't mix them up.

Sports invented in the USA.Basketball: James Naismith, a Canadian, invented it in 1891 in Springfield, Massachusetts. The first games used peach baskets.
Sports invented in the USA.Volleyball: William Morgan created it in 1895 at a Massachusetts YMCA as a gentler game than basketball, calling it mintonette.
Sports invented in the USA.American football: Evolved from rugby and soccer on college campuses. The first intercollegiate game was Rutgers against Princeton in 1869.
Sports invented in the USA.Softball: Began in 1887 in Chicago as an indoor game, played with a boxing glove tied into a ball.
Sports invented in the USA.Pickleball: Invented in 1965 on Bainbridge Island, Washington. The name's origin is disputed between a dog named Pickles and a pickle boat.
Sports invented in the USA.Racquetball: Joe Sobek invented it around 1950 as paddle rackets, played in a handball court in Connecticut.
Sports invented in the USA.Ultimate frisbee: Developed in 1968 at a New Jersey high school. Players call their own fouls under a spirit of the game.
Sports invented in the USA.Kickball: A playground game born in early 20th-century Cincinnati as kick baseball, where you kick a rubber ball instead of hitting one.
Sports invented in the USA.Paintball: First played in 1981 in New Hampshire, with markers designed to tag trees and cattle at a distance.
Sports invented in the USA.Wiffle ball: Invented in 1953 in Connecticut by David Mullany. The perforated plastic ball curves easily, so pitchers need little strength.
Sports invented in the USA.Disc golf: Standardised in the 1970s by Ed Headrick, who also refined the modern Frisbee. Players throw into chain baskets.
Sports invented in the USA.Ice hockey: It grew up in Canada, with early organised games in Montreal in 1875.
Sports invented in the USA.Soccer: English in origin. The Football Association codified the rules in 1863.
Sports invented in the USA.Rugby: Named after Rugby School in England. The William Webb Ellis story is probably a myth.
Sports invented in the USA.Cricket: English in origin, with references from the 1500s, and not American.
Sports invented in the USA.Tennis: It descends from French jeu de paume, and modern lawn tennis was patented by Major Walter Wingfield in Britain.
Sports invented in the USA.Golf: It's Scotland's game, played at St Andrews since the 1400s.
Sports invented in the USA.Badminton: Named for Badminton House in England. It grew from the Indian game poona, played by British officers.
Sports invented in the USA.Squash: Invented at Harrow School in England in the 19th century and named for the soft ball that squashes on impact.
Sports invented in the USA.Table tennis: A Victorian English after-dinner game, ping-pong. It has been Olympic since 1988.
Sports invented in the USA.Judo: Created in Japan in 1882 by Jigoro Kano, and the name means gentle way.
Sports invented in the USA.Curling: Scottish, with the oldest known stone dated 1511.
Sports invented in the USA.Polo: Possibly the world's oldest team sport, with Persian and Central Asian roots over 2,000 years old.
Sports invented in the USA.Netball: It evolved from basketball in 1890s England, with no dribbling and no running with the ball.

Figures of Chinese mythology.Sun Wukong: The Monkey King of 'Journey to the West' was born from a stone, and steals immortality peaches before Buddha pins him under a mountain.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Jade Emperor: The ruler of Heaven in Chinese folk religion, who is said to have held a race of animals that gave the zodiac its order.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Chang'e: The Moon goddess, who drank the elixir of immortality and flew to the moon, where a jade rabbit keeps her company; China's lunar probes carry her name.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Nuwa: The creator goddess who shaped humans from yellow clay, and repaired the sky with colored stones after it was torn.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Pangu: The first being, who separated heaven and earth by growing for 18,000 years; after his death, his body became mountains, rivers and sky.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Houyi: The archer who shot down nine of ten suns that were scorching the world, saving humanity.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Nian: A beast that attacked villages at New Year; it feared red, loud noises and fire, which supposedly started the tradition of red decorations and firecrackers.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Qilin: A gentle, hoofed creature, with scales and a horn, whose appearance signals a wise ruler; often translated 'Chinese unicorn'.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Erlang Shen: A god with a third eye on his forehead and a hound, who fought Sun Wukong, the only one nearly able to beat him.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Dragon King: Four Dragon Kings rule the seas and rain in Chinese myth; villagers prayed to them in droughts and floods.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Zhong Kui: The demon-queller, who is shown with a fierce beard, and whose picture is hung at New Year or Dragon Boat Festival to protect houses.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Amaterasu: A trap: the sun goddess is Japanese, though she hid in a cave much like Chinese myths of the sun.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Susanoo: A trap: the Japanese storm god, brother of Amaterasu, killed the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Izanagi: A trap: Japan's creator god, who with his wife Izanami formed the islands, is not Chinese.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Kitsune: A trap: Japanese fox spirits grow more tails with age, up to nine; China has a fox spirit too, the huli jing.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Tengu: A trap: this beaked mountain goblin of Japan has nothing to do with Chinese myth.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Oni: A trap: Japanese horned ogres, driven away at Setsubun by thrown beans, not Chinese.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Anubis: A trap: the jackal-headed Egyptian god of embalming has no part in Chinese myth.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Thor: A trap: the Norse thunder god swings the hammer Mjolnir; Chinese thunder belongs to Leigong.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Medusa: A trap: the snake-haired Gorgon is from Greek myth, and could turn onlookers to stone.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Baba Yaga: A trap: the witch with a hut on chicken legs is from Slavic folklore.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Quetzalcoatl: A trap: the Aztec Feathered Serpent is from Mesoamerica, though Chinese dragons are also sky serpents.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Gilgamesh: A trap: the hero king of Uruk is Mesopotamian; his epic was written on clay tablets over 4,000 years ago.
Figures of Chinese mythology.Kappa: A trap: the Japanese river imp with a water-filled dish on its head is not Chinese.

Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Maya: Built tall stone pyramids and developed a full writing system and a precise calendar. Their cities were in the Yucatan and Central America, and the Maya people live there today.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Aztec: Their island capital Tenochtitlan, now under Mexico City, held about 200,000 people when the Spanish arrived in 1519. They paid for it with tribute from conquered peoples.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Inca: Ruled the largest empire in pre-Columbian America from the Andes. They had no writing, but kept records on knotted cords called quipu.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Olmec: Often called the mother culture of Mesoamerica. They carved colossal stone heads up to about 3 m tall and flourished from roughly 1200 BC.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Toltec: A Mesoamerican culture centred on Tula, in central Mexico. The later Aztecs revered the Toltecs as master craftsmen and the source of all civilization.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Zapotec: They built Monte Albán on a levelled mountaintop in Oaxaca and were among the earliest in the Americas to use writing and a calendar.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Moche: A Peruvian coastal culture, active around AD 100 to 800, famous for portrait pottery and richly decorated tombs, such as that of the Lord of Sipán.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Nazca: Known for the huge desert lines in Peru, including a hummingbird and monkey, made by clearing dark stones. They are visible best from the air.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Mixtec: Oaxacan neighbours of the Zapotecs, renowned for exquisite goldwork and painted folding-book manuscripts, known as codices.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Sumerians: Mesopotamian, not American. They are credited with inventing cuneiform writing in about 3400 BC, in what is now Iraq.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Babylonians: They lived in Mesopotamia, in Iraq, and developed a base-60 number system. That is why we have 60 minutes in an hour.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Assyrians: A Mesopotamian military power whose library at Nineveh holds thousands of clay tablets, including the Epic of Gilgamesh.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Hittites: A Bronze Age power in Anatolia (modern Turkey) and among the first to work iron widely. They fought Egypt at Kadesh around 1274 BC.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Phoenicians: Seafaring traders from the Levant, whose alphabet is the ancestor of Greek and Latin letters. Their civilization is Old World.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Minoans: A Bronze Age culture on Crete, famed for the palace of Knossos and bull-leaping frescoes. They lived in Europe, thousands of miles from the Americas.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Etruscans: A culture in what is now Tuscany that influenced early Rome. Italy, not the Americas.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Carthaginians: From Carthage in North Africa, Hannibal's people. Phoenician colonists, they fought three Punic Wars with Rome.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Persians: Their empire spanned West Asia, Egypt and beyond, and was known for its imperial road system. Eastern Hemisphere, nothing American.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Celts: Iron Age peoples across Europe, in Gaul, Britain and Ireland. Their art and languages survive, but they are European.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Mongols: The Mongol Empire of Genghis Khan became the largest contiguous land empire in history. It reached across Asia and into Europe.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Khmer: The Cambodian empire that built Angkor Wat. It belongs to Southeast Asia, not the Americas.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Harappans: Also called the Indus Valley civilisation, in modern Pakistan and India. Their cities had planned streets and drains around 2500 BC. Their script is undeciphered.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Spartans: Greek warriors from Laconia, trained from boyhood. They are European, and a famous stand at Thermopylae came in 480 BC.
Ancient civilizations of the Americas.Vikings: Norse seafarers who did reach North America around AD 1000 at L'Anse aux Meadows, but they were no American civilization.

From feudal Japan.Samurai: Warriors who served daimyo lords. Their privileged class was abolished in the 1870s Meiji reforms.
From feudal Japan.Shogun: A military ruler acting in the emperor's name. Emperors stayed as figureheads in Kyoto for centuries, until 1868.
From feudal Japan.Daimyo: Regional lords with their own samurai armies. The Tokugawa made them spend alternate years in Edo, keeping their families there as hostages.
From feudal Japan.Ninja: Spies and saboteurs. The all-black outfit mostly comes from theater, where stagehands in black were treated as invisible.
From feudal Japan.Katana: The curved sword's smiths layered and hammered steel, giving a hard cutting edge and a flexible spine.
From feudal Japan.Ronin: A samurai with no master. The word means wave man, as if drifting; the tale of the 47 Ronin is Japan's most famous revenge story.
From feudal Japan.Bushido: The way of the warrior. Much of the code was written down in the peaceful Edo era, after the fighting had mostly ended.
From feudal Japan.Geisha: Skilled performers of music, dance and conversation, not what many outsiders assume. The first geisha were actually men.
From feudal Japan.Kabuki: It began in 17th-century Kyoto with a female dancer, but women were later banned. All-male casts remain the tradition today.
From feudal Japan.Haiku: A tiny poem traditionally of 17 sounds. Matsuo Basho raised it to an art in the 1600s, and it was long called hokku.
From feudal Japan.Kimono: The word means thing to wear. It is wrapped left side over right, and right over left only for dressing the dead.
From feudal Japan.Kung fu: A Chinese martial art, not Japanese. Japan's own traditions include judo, karate and kendo.
From feudal Japan.Terracotta Army: Thousands of clay soldiers guard China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, buried around 210 BC. Chinese, not Japanese.
From feudal Japan.Great Wall: China's defensive walls were built over many centuries. Japan had castles, but no wall like it.
From feudal Japan.Mandarin: China's main language and the original name of its imperial officials. Not from Japan.
From feudal Japan.Gladiator: A Roman arena fighter, not a Japanese one. Rome's games ended long before Japan's samurai era began.
From feudal Japan.Knight: Europe's feudal counterpart to the samurai: a mounted warrior sworn to a lord. Similar idea, a world away.
From feudal Japan.Viking: Scandinavian raiders and traders of roughly 800 to 1100. They never reached Japan.
From feudal Japan.Taj Mahal: Built in India by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Not Japanese.
From feudal Japan.Kimchi: Korea's fermented cabbage staple, with hundreds of varieties. Not Japanese cuisine.
From feudal Japan.Hanbok: Korea's traditional dress, known for its bright colors and high-waisted skirts. Not Japan's kimono.
From feudal Japan.Dim sum: Small Cantonese dishes served with tea, from southern China. Not Japanese.
From feudal Japan.Mahjong: A Chinese tile game that became hugely popular worldwide in the 1920s. Not from feudal Japan.
From feudal Japan.Sitar: A long-necked Indian stringed instrument, made famous in the West by Ravi Shankar. Not Japanese.

From ancient India.Indus Valley: A Bronze Age civilization of about 2600 to 1900 BC across modern Pakistan and India. Its cities had planned streets and drains, but its script is still undeciphered.
From ancient India.Mohenjo-daro: One of the Indus Valley's largest cities, with a Great Bath and brick drainage. Its name means 'Mound of the Dead' in Sindhi.
From ancient India.Harappa: An Indus city in Punjab, one of the first discovered in the 1920s. Its bricks were later carried off to build railway tracks.
From ancient India.Ashoka: The Mauryan emperor who, after a bloody war in Kalinga, embraced Buddhism and carved moral edicts on pillars across his empire.
From ancient India.Maurya Empire: India's first great empire, uniting most of the subcontinent around 320 BC. Its capital was Pataliputra.
From ancient India.Chandragupta: Founder of the Maurya Empire, who took power in about 320 BC. Tradition says he ended his life as a Jain monk.
From ancient India.Sanskrit: An ancient language of India, ancestor of many modern ones, and distantly related to Latin, Greek and English.
From ancient India.Gupta Empire: The dynasty of roughly the fourth to sixth centuries, often called a golden age of art, math and science. The concept of zero flourished then.
From ancient India.Taxila: An ancient centre of learning near modern Islamabad, said to have taught Chanakya, the Mauryan strategist.
From ancient India.Nalanda: A great Buddhist university in Bihar, which at its peak hosted thousands of students and monks. It was destroyed in the 1190s.
From ancient India.Taj Mahal: Trap: the white marble tomb in Agra, built in the 1600s. It's Mughal, nearly two thousand years after ancient India.
From ancient India.Akbar: Trap: a Mughal emperor of the 1500s who tolerated many religions. He ruled long after ancient India's golden ages.
From ancient India.Red Fort: Trap: a red sandstone fortress in Delhi, built in the 1600s by the Mughals, not ancient.
From ancient India.Gandhi: Trap: leader of India's independence in the 20th century, who led peaceful resistance. Modern, not ancient.
From ancient India.Babylon: Trap: a Mesopotamian city in modern Iraq, known for its Hanging Gardens. It lies far west of India.
From ancient India.Persepolis: Trap: a ceremonial capital of the Persian Empire in modern Iran. It belongs to a neighbouring culture.
From ancient India.Angkor Wat: Trap: a Cambodian temple complex, originally Hindu and built by the Khmer in the 1100s, so Southeast Asian and medieval.
From ancient India.Shah Jahan: Trap: the Mughal emperor who built the Taj Mahal for his wife, in the 1600s. Not ancient.
From ancient India.British Raj: Trap: Britain's rule over India, from 1858 to 1947. It's thousands of years after the ancient period.
From ancient India.East India Company: Trap: a British trading company founded in 1600 that came to control much of India. It came long after antiquity.
From ancient India.Bollywood: Trap: the Hindi film industry based in Mumbai, which is a twentieth-century phenomenon.
From ancient India.Mughal Empire: Trap: the Muslim dynasty that ruled northern India from 1526 until the 1850s, quite late and not ancient.
From ancient India.Tipu Sultan: Trap: the 18th-century ruler of Mysore, nicknamed the Tiger of Mysore. He fought the British, but long after antiquity.
From ancient India.Victoria Memorial: Trap: a white marble museum in Kolkata, completed in 1921 to honour Queen Victoria, thus colonial and modern.

Things that have pedals.Bicycle: A bicycle pedal drives the rear wheel through a chain, and the first pedal-driven bike appeared in the 1860s in France.
Things that have pedals.Piano: A grand piano usually has three pedals, and the right one, the sustain pedal, lifts all the dampers so notes ring on.
Things that have pedals.Pedal bin: The foot pedal lets you open the lid without touching it, which is why it is popular in kitchens and clinics.
Things that have pedals.Sewing machine: Many old sewing machines were driven by a treadle pedal that rocked under the foot, and electric motors replaced them in the early 1900s.
Things that have pedals.Car: A manual car has three pedals, and the left one, the clutch, disengages the engine so gears can be changed.
Things that have pedals.Drum kit: A standard kit has a bass drum pedal that swings a beater, and many also have a hi-hat pedal that opens and closes the cymbals.
Things that have pedals.Pipe organ: Organs have pedalboards played with the feet, and they control the lowest notes, some of which are too deep for most speakers.
Things that have pedals.Pedal boat: A pedal boat turns a paddle wheel or propeller by foot power, and it is a popular tourist rental on calm lakes.
Things that have pedals.Tricycle: A tricycle has pedals mounted directly on the front wheel, which is why children's models steer and pedal with the same wheel.
Things that have pedals.Concert harp: A concert harp has seven pedals that change the pitch of each note name, and they let a harpist play in any key.
Things that have pedals.Exercise bike: It has pedals but no wheels that go anywhere, so it provides the cardio of cycling without ever leaving the room.
Things that have pedals.Unicycle: A unicycle has pedals attached right to the wheel's axle, so there's no freewheel and the rider can't coast.
Things that have pedals.Skateboard: You push off with your foot on the ground; a skateboard has no pedals, and the board itself steers by leaning.
Things that have pedals.Kick scooter: A kick scooter is pushed with one foot against the ground, so there are no pedals at all.
Things that have pedals.Toaster: Its lever is pushed down by hand, not a foot pedal, though some old commercial toasters did use a lever mechanism.
Things that have pedals.Violin: A violin is played with a bow and fingers and has no pedals; the foot is used only to keep time.
Things that have pedals.Guitar: No pedals on the guitar itself, but guitarists often plug into effects pedals on the floor, which is a sneaky trap.
Things that have pedals.Trumpet: A trumpet has three piston valves worked by the fingers, not pedals, though larger brass horns sometimes have extra valves.
Things that have pedals.Flute: A flute uses keys and a mouth hole and has no pedals, a design that dates back tens of thousands of years in some forms.
Things that have pedals.Canoe: A canoe is moved by paddles in the hands, not pedals, though pedal-driven kayaks do exist.
Things that have pedals.Roller skates: Roller skates are strapped to the feet and have wheels but no pedals; the skater pushes off sideways.
Things that have pedals.Wheelchair: A manual wheelchair is propelled by pushing the rims with the hands, with no pedals, apart from footrests.
Things that have pedals.Sled: A sled slides downhill by gravity and has no pedals, and some are steered by shifting the weight.
Things that have pedals.Hoverboard: A hoverboard is steered by leaning and has pads under the feet, and these are not pedals.

Things with a spout.Teapot: The spout is angled so tea pours smoothly without dribbling, and a tiny air hole in the lid keeps the flow steady.
Things with a spout.Kettle: Whistling kettles use a steam-driven reed in the spout, a trick that dates to the early 1900s.
Things with a spout.Watering can: A rose, the perforated nozzle on the spout, breaks the water into a gentle shower that won't flatten seedlings.
Things with a spout.Jug: The pouring lip on many jugs is called a spout, designed so liquid hugs the edge instead of running down the side.
Things with a spout.Gravy boat: The low, narrow spout lets sauce be poured precisely, and some designs have a second compartment under it to keep it warm.
Things with a spout.Oil can: Its long, thin spout lets mechanics reach tight joints, and the pump-style types squirt a precise drop of oil.
Things with a spout.Gas can: Modern ones have child-resistant spouts, because spills and fumes from spouts without vents were a common hazard.
Things with a spout.Faucet: The spout shapes the flow, and a small mesh aerator inside mixes air into the water to make it smoother and save water.
Things with a spout.Measuring jug: The spout helps pour accurately, and the markings are read at eye level because liquid curves slightly at the edge.
Things with a spout.Coffee pot: A classic stovetop moka pot pushes water up through grounds and out of a central spout, invented in Italy in 1933.
Things with a spout.Juice carton: A folded paper spout lets you pour without a cap, a clever origami-like design in gable-top cartons.
Things with a spout.Plate: A plate is flat with no spout, and sauces on it usually need a gravy boat instead.
Things with a spout.Bowl: A bowl's rim is round all the way, with no spout, though the old 'pouring bowl' with a lip is called a pitcher.
Things with a spout.Mug: Mugs have a handle but no spout, which is why they're tricky to pour from without spilling.
Things with a spout.Wine glass: The wide bowl and narrow rim concentrate aromas, but there's no spout, which is why decanters were invented for pouring.
Things with a spout.Tumbler: A tumbler is just a flat-bottomed drinking glass, rim only, and the name comes from older rounded-bottom glasses that tumbled.
Things with a spout.Cup: A cup's rim is for sipping, not pouring; adding a spout makes it a sippy cup, popular with toddlers.
Things with a spout.Ladle: A ladle can have a pouring lip on its rim, but it is a spoon-like scoop rather than a spouted container.
Things with a spout.Colander: It has holes, not a spout, and the name comes from the Latin colare, meaning to strain.
Things with a spout.Frying pan: A frying pan has a pouring lip, but a true spout is a tube or channel, which pans lack.
Things with a spout.Sieve: A sieve sorts by size through its mesh, with no spout, and has been used to separate grain since ancient times.
Things with a spout.Spoon: A spoon is a scoop with no spout, among the oldest tools, and spoons made of wood or bone date back to prehistory.
Things with a spout.Fork: Forks were once seen as scandalous in Europe; a Byzantine princess's use of one in Venice in the 11th century shocked guests.
Things with a spout.Ramekin: A ramekin is a small baking dish for soufflés and crème brûlée with no spout, and the name comes from a French cheese dish.

Fermented foods.Yogurt: Yogurt gets its tang from bacteria turning milk sugar into lactic acid, and the word itself is Turkish.
Fermented foods.Kefir: Kefir is made with 'grains' that are really clumps of bacteria and yeast, a tradition from the Caucasus.
Fermented foods.Sauerkraut: Sauerkraut means 'sour cabbage' in German, and sailors carried it on long voyages to ward off scurvy.
Fermented foods.Kimchi: Korea has hundreds of kimchi varieties, and families traditionally made a year's supply together in a ritual called kimjang.
Fermented foods.Kombucha: Kombucha is tea fermented by a SCOBY, a rubbery pad of bacteria and yeast that floats on top.
Fermented foods.Miso: Miso is soybeans fermented with koji mold, and darker misos are aged longer and taste stronger.
Fermented foods.Tempeh: Tempeh from Indonesia binds soybeans into a firm cake using a Rhizopus mold.
Fermented foods.Soy sauce: Soy sauce is brewed for months from soybeans, wheat, salt and koji mold.
Fermented foods.Sourdough bread: Sourdough rises on wild yeast and bacteria, and some starters have been kept alive for generations.
Fermented foods.Natto: Natto is sticky, stringy fermented soybeans eaten in Japan, famous for its strong smell.
Fermented foods.Vinegar: Vinegar forms when bacteria turn alcohol into acetic acid, and the word comes from French for 'sour wine'.
Fermented foods.Salami: Salami is cured and fermented, with lactic bacteria lowering its acidity before it is air-dried.
