Fermented foods.Tofu: Tofu is made by curdling soy milk, much like cheese, not by fermentation.
Fermented foods.Hummus: Hummus blends chickpeas, tahini and lemon with no fermentation, and 'hummus' is simply Arabic for chickpeas.
Fermented foods.Milk: Plain milk is not fermented; it becomes yogurt or kefir only after bacteria get to work.
Fermented foods.Pasta: Pasta dough is flour and water, shaped and dried, with no fermentation involved.
Fermented foods.Tortilla: Corn tortillas use masa, made by soaking corn in limewater, a process called nixtamalization, not fermenting.
Fermented foods.White rice: White rice is simply milled and cooked, though rice can be fermented into sake or rice vinegar.
Fermented foods.Granola: Granola is baked oats, nuts and sweetener; its crunch comes from toasting, not microbes.
Fermented foods.Guacamole: Guacamole is mashed avocado, and the name comes from Nahuatl for 'avocado sauce'.
Fermented foods.Popcorn: Popcorn pops when water inside the kernel turns to steam and bursts it, no microbes needed.
Fermented foods.Applesauce: Applesauce is cooked apples; ferment the juice instead and you get cider.
Fermented foods.Peanut butter: Peanut butter is ground roasted peanuts, not fermented; the oil that separates is natural.
Fermented foods.Edamame: Edamame are young soybeans, steamed fresh; ferment mature ones and you get natto or miso.

Things an astronaut needs in space.Spacesuit: A spacesuit is a miniature spacecraft that gives oxygen, pressure, and protection from extreme temperatures, with a dozen layers.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Space helmet: A space helmet has a gold-coated visor that shields astronauts' eyes from the intense, unfiltered sunlight.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Oxygen tank: Astronauts breathe oxygen supplied from tanks or the station's own supply, and the suit's pressure is much lower than Earth's for flexibility.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Rocket: A rocket is needed because reaching orbit takes a speed of about 28,000 kilometers per hour.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Freeze-dried food: Space food is often freeze-dried to save weight and last long, and astronauts add water to eat it.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Safety tether: A tether keeps astronauts attached during spacewalks, because without gravity a loose tool or person drifts away.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Radio: Sound can't travel through the vacuum of space, so astronauts talk by radio, which carries signals at the speed of light.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Space station: The International Space Station orbits about 400 kilometers up, circling Earth roughly every 90 minutes.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Toolkit: Astronauts carry special tools made for gloved hands, and tools are tethered, since any loose one can float away.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Gloves: Space gloves are among the toughest parts of the suit to design, since astronauts need to feel while protected.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Umbrella: There is no rain in the vacuum of space, and an umbrella could not keep out any danger there, like radiation.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Surfboard: Surfing needs ocean waves and gravity, and neither exists in the weightless vacuum of an orbiting station.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Kite: A kite needs air moving past it to fly, and in the vacuum of space there is none, so it would just float.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Snorkel: A snorkel is a tube for breathing air at the water's surface, and in space there is no air to breathe through it.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Snow shovel: A snow shovel is for clearing snowfall, and there is no weather at all in orbit, which is just vacuum, sunlight, and floating dust.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Bicycle: Astronauts do pedal a stationary exercise bike in orbit to keep muscles strong, but you can't ride a bike around space.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Fishing rod: A fishing rod needs water and fish, though astronauts have actually kept fish aboard the station for research.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Sailboat: Sailboats rely on wind, which space lacks, though some probes use solar sails that push on sunlight instead.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Skateboard: A skateboard needs gravity and a ground to roll on, and a floating astronaut has neither; in orbit, everything just drifts.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Hot air balloon: A hot air balloon floats because warm air is lighter than the cooler air around it, and space has no air at all.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Lawnmower: There's no lawn in orbit, though astronauts have grown lettuce and zinnias on the International Space Station.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Beach ball: Astronauts would have a fun time with a ball in microgravity, but it isn't needed, and it would drift around rather than bounce.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Garden hose: In space, water doesn't flow down but forms floating blobs, so a hose would be useless for watering anything.
Things an astronaut needs in space.Roller skates: Roller skates need gravity and friction against the ground, and a drifting astronaut has neither.

Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Fly a kite: Ben Franklin's kite stunt was far riskier than it sounds; in 1753 a scientist repeating similar experiments in Russia was killed by lightning.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Go swimming: Lightning striking water spreads its current across the surface, so swimmers can be hurt well away from the actual strike point.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Play golf: Golfers are tall, in open ground and holding metal clubs; lightning is among the leading weather-related causes of death on courses.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Stand under a tree: Sheltering under a tree is the classic mistake: current can leap from the trunk to you, and trees are often the tallest target around.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Climb a flagpole: Lightning seeks the highest conductive point, which makes a flagpole nearly an invitation, especially when it's metal.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Go fishing: A long carbon-fibre rod held up near open water is about the worst gear in a storm; fishing is among the riskiest outdoor activities.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Climb a mountain: Exposed peaks and ridges put you the nearest to the cloud base, and mountain rescue teams warn to descend before storms build, usually afternoons.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Stand in a field: In a flat open field you can become the tallest object around, and a strike's current can travel through the ground to you.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Sit on a roof: Roofs are high and exposed, and metal gutters and wet surfaces can carry current from a strike to anyone sitting there.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Go canoeing: Open water has no cover at all, and a canoe puts you as the tallest object for a long way around.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Read a book: Indoors a book is safe: a building acts as a shelter, though staying away from corded phones and plumbing is wise during a storm.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Watch a movie: A trap: movies are safe, but plugged-in electronics aren't; a nearby strike can send a surge down the wiring and fry the TV.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Take a nap: Napping indoors is fine, since a building directs lightning's current through its wiring and plumbing around you.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Bake cookies: Baking is safe as long as you avoid the sink; plumbing can carry a strike's current, so skip washing up during storms.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Play board games: Board games fit the storm; officials suggest staying inside 30 minutes after the last thunder you hear.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Do a puzzle: A puzzle on a table well away from windows is a perfect storm activity, with no outdoors involved.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Knit a scarf: Knitting involves only wood and yarn and keeps you indoors, which is the whole point of storm safety.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Drink cocoa: Cocoa is safe, since a building's walls protect you; you hear thunder only if the strike is close enough to be a risk.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Cuddle a cat: Petting a cat inside is safe; thunder is heard within about 10 miles, which is close enough for an outdoor pet to be at risk.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Write a letter: Writing a letter is safe, but with a corded phone nearby remember that strikes can travel through phone lines.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Build a pillow fort: A pillow fort indoors is a fine option; a car works too, as its metal shell conducts a strike around you.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Play cards: Playing cards is safe indoors, and a simple rule says if you can hear thunder, you're close enough to be struck.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Do homework: Homework is a fine storm activity; the safest place is inside a fully enclosed building with wiring and plumbing.
Bad things to do in a lightning storm.Eat popcorn: Popcorn indoors is safe, and a hard-topped car is too: its metal shell carries a strike around you, a Faraday-cage effect.

Things on a business card.Name: The business card descends from 17th-century visiting cards, and the name still sits at the top, big and bold.
Things on a business card.Job title: A job title tells people your role, and in Japan the formal card exchange, meishi koukan, follows careful etiquette.
Things on a business card.Phone number: Phone numbers still appear on cards even as email dominates, because they're quick to dial and need no typing.
Things on a business card.Email address: Email appeared on cards in the 1990s, replacing the fax numbers that used to sit in the same spot.
Things on a business card.Company logo: The logo makes the card recognisable, and designers often use a spare, uncluttered layout around it.
Things on a business card.Office address: Postal addresses are less common now, though they remain on cards for legal and shipping needs.
Things on a business card.Website: Websites became standard on cards by the late 1990s, as a place to learn more than a card could hold.
Things on a business card.QR code: Invented in 1994 by Denso Wave, a Toyota supplier, QR codes now link cards to profiles and contact files.
Things on a business card.Social handle: LinkedIn or other social handles on cards let people find you online, which is handy for networking.
Things on a business card.Date of birth: A birth date is private information that fraudsters use for identity theft, so you never print it on a card.
Things on a business card.Salary: Pay is confidential, and a card showing your salary would make for an awkward networking event.
Things on a business card.Blood type: Blood type matters in emergencies, and it appears on some ID and dog tags, but not on a business card.
Things on a business card.Shoe size: Shoe size is useful to a shoe shop, not to someone deciding whether to hire or phone you.
Things on a business card.Bank PIN: A PIN is a secret code, and printing one on a card you hand out would be a disaster.
Things on a business card.Password: Passwords are secrets; sharing them on a handout is a security failure.
Things on a business card.Star sign: A star sign isn't useful for business, though some people do mention it in dating profiles.
Things on a business card.Home Wi-Fi code: A Wi-Fi code gives access to your home network; guests get it in person, not on your professional card.
Things on a business card.Medical history: Medical details are protected personal data in many places, such as under HIPAA in the US.
Things on a business card.Diary entry: A diary is private writing, so never put one on a card you hand to strangers.
Things on a business card.Grocery list: A grocery list may help your shopping, but a card is a tiny space for contact details only.
Things on a business card.Credit score: A credit score is financial data lenders use, so it's kept private, not printed on a card.
Things on a business card.Body weight: Body weight is private, and few things are less relevant to business contacts.
Things on a business card.Passport number: A passport number is sensitive identity data that fraudsters want, so it must never be printed on a card.
Things on a business card.Exam grades: Grades matter for school, but cards list current roles, not marks from long ago.

Characters in A Christmas Carol.Ebenezer Scrooge: The miser's name, taken from a gravestone Dickens may have seen, became a word for stinginess, and "Bah! Humbug!" his catchphrase.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Bob Cratchit: Scrooge's clerk earns about fifteen shillings a week, and still raises a toast to his boss at Christmas dinner.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Tiny Tim: The crippled youngest Cratchit survives in the story's new future; Dickens's tale made him a symbol of Christmas kindness.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Jacob Marley: Scrooge's dead partner appears dragging a chain of cash boxes and ledgers, which he says he forged "link by link" in life.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Mr. Fezziwig: Scrooge's old employer throws a joyful Christmas ball, showing that a boss can make staff happy for very little money.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Fred: Scrooge's cheerful nephew invites him to Christmas dinner every year and never stops forgiving his uncle's rudeness.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Belle: Scrooge's former fiancée leaves him because his love of money has replaced his love for her; she later has a happy family.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Mrs. Cratchit: She calls Scrooge "an odious, stingy, hard, unfeeling man" but joins the toast anyway, and serves the family's tiny pudding proudly.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Fan: Scrooge's beloved younger sister, Fred's mother, rescues him from school and dies young, which is why Fred matters to him.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Oliver Twist: Dickens's workhouse orphan comes from a different novel, written five years before A Christmas Carol.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Fagin: The villain who trains child thieves belongs to Oliver Twist, not to Scrooge's Christmas Eve.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Pip: The orphan of Great Expectations is a different Dickens hero, who learns his own lesson about money and status.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Miss Havisham: The rotting-wedding-cake recluse is from Great Expectations, not the Christmas ghost story.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Uriah Heep: The scheming "umble" clerk is a David Copperfield character, a very different clerk from kind Bob Cratchit.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.The Grinch: Dr. Seuss's green Christmas-hater of 1957 is a trap here: he steals Christmas in Whoville, not in Dickens's London.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Cindy Lou Who: The tiny girl who catches the Grinch is from Dr. Seuss's 1957 book and not from Dickens.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Santa Claus: Though Christmas now means Santa, he doesn't appear in A Christmas Carol; its spirit of Christmas Present is a giant in a green robe.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Rudolph: The red-nosed reindeer was invented in 1939 as a department-store giveaway booklet, almost a century after Dickens.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Frosty: The snowman who comes to life when a magic hat is put on him is from a 1950 song, not from Dickens's story.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Jack Frost: The folkloric winter sprite who paints windows with ice has no role in Scrooge's Christmas.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Clara: The girl in The Nutcracker ballet gets her toy nutcracker at a Christmas party, but she is not in the Dickens tale.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.The Nutcracker: The 1892 ballet and its toy soldier celebrate Christmas but come from E.T.A. Hoffmann's tale, not Dickens.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Mr. Micawber: Always expecting "something to turn up", he is a David Copperfield character, not one of Scrooge's circle.
Characters in A Christmas Carol.Little Nell: Dickens's doomed child heroine is from The Old Curiosity Shop, not A Christmas Carol.

Characters in Little Women.Jo March: Louisa May Alcott modelled this fiery, ink-stained writer on herself; Jo sells her hair to help the family.
Characters in Little Women.Meg March: The oldest sister longs for fine things but marries a poor tutor, John Brooke, for love.
Characters in Little Women.Beth March: The shy musical sister catches scarlet fever from a poor family she helps, and her death is among literature's best-known tearjerkers.
Characters in Little Women.Amy March: The youngest sister burns Jo's manuscript in anger, which many fans still can't forgive, but she grows into a skilled artist.
Characters in Little Women.Marmee: The sisters' mother, based on Alcott's own mother, runs the household while Mr. March is away at the Civil War.
Characters in Little Women.Laurie: The wealthy boy next door, Theodore Laurence, loves Jo, but she refuses him and he marries Amy.
Characters in Little Women.Aunt March: The sharp-tongued, rich aunt who employs Jo as her companion eventually leaves her house to her.
Characters in Little Women.Professor Bhaer: The kindly older German professor in New York becomes Jo's husband and encourages her to write seriously.
Characters in Little Women.John Brooke: Laurie's tutor, a poor but honest man, marries Meg and shows the family that love matters more than wealth.
Characters in Little Women.Hannah: The family's loyal Irish servant helps the Marches through hard times, quietly holding the household together.
Characters in Little Women.Mr. Laurence: Laurie's grandfather, the lonely rich neighbour, befriends Beth and gives her a piano.
Characters in Little Women.Anne Shirley: L. M. Montgomery's red-haired chatterbox lives in Prince Edward Island, not Concord, Massachusetts.
Characters in Little Women.Diana Barry: Anne's "bosom friend" is from Anne of Green Gables, not the March family.
Characters in Little Women.Gilbert Blythe: The boy Anne famously hits over the head with a slate is from Anne of Green Gables.
Characters in Little Women.Marilla Cuthbert: The stern, soft-hearted adoptive guardian is from Anne of Green Gables, not Little Women.
Characters in Little Women.Pollyanna: Eleanor Porter's relentlessly cheerful orphan gave her name to excessive optimism, but she isn't in Alcott's book.
Characters in Little Women.Heidi: Johanna Spyri's mountain girl lives in the Swiss Alps, far from the Marches' Massachusetts.
Characters in Little Women.Mary Lennox: The sour young girl who finds a hidden garden is from The Secret Garden, set in Yorkshire.
Characters in Little Women.Dickon: The kind boy who talks to animals in The Secret Garden is not part of Alcott's story.
Characters in Little Women.Laura Ingalls: Wilder's real-life prairie girl lived in the Midwest wilderness, a different sort of childhood from the Marches'.
Characters in Little Women.Scout Finch: The Alabama tomboy of To Kill a Mockingbird is not a March, but a close American cousin of Jo.
Characters in Little Women.Elizabeth Bennet: Austen's heroine belongs to Regency England, not Civil War New England, though the March sisters adored Austen-style romance.
Characters in Little Women.Jane Eyre: Brontë's governess is from 1840s Yorkshire; Alcott's Jo and her sisters read plenty of English novels, though.
Characters in Little Women.Dorothy Gale: The Kansas girl of The Wizard of Oz is from L. Frank Baum's 1900 fantasy.

Parts of a book.Spine: Titles are printed on it so books can be found on shelves, and US and UK titles read top to bottom, while many European ones read bottom to top.
Parts of a book.Cover: Penguin launched cheap paperbacks in 1935, color-coding the covers by genre: orange for fiction, green for crime.
Parts of a book.Preface: Written by the author about the book's creation, while a foreword is typically by someone else.
Parts of a book.Index: The alphabetical guide at the back; nonfiction ones are often made by a professional indexer, not the author.
Parts of a book.Chapter: From Latin "caput", head, because early chapters were simply numbered headings in a long text.
Parts of a book.Prologue: Greek for "before word", it sets up background before the story begins, and is separate from the first chapter.
Parts of a book.Epilogue: It ends the story, often years later, like Harry Potter's "Nineteen Years Later" scene on the platform.
Parts of a book.Appendix: Latin for "attachment", it carries extra material at the back and is unrelated to the body organ except in name.
Parts of a book.Glossary: A list of specialized terms, from Greek "glossa", meaning tongue or language, usually near the end.
Parts of a book.Dust jacket: Early ones were disposable wrappers from the early 1800s, and first-edition jackets can be worth far more than the book.
Parts of a book.Footnote: Notes at the page's bottom, which Gibbon's Decline and Fall made famously witty and opinionated.
Parts of a book.Dedication: Vladimir Nabokov dedicated most of his books to his wife Véra, and many authors use this page to thank someone.
Parts of a book.Bibliography: From Greek for "book writing", it lists the sources an author consulted, and sits at the very back.
Parts of a book.Overture: An opera's or musical's opening instrumental piece, so it belongs to the stage and not to a book.
Parts of a book.Intermission: A break in the middle of a show, a theater term, and a book simply has no counterpart for it.
Parts of a book.Encore: French for "again", though French audiences actually shout "bis" instead, for a performer's extra number.
Parts of a book.Refrain: The repeated lines of a song, so a part of music, even though poems also use refrains now and then.
Parts of a book.Interval: What British audiences call the pause in a show, and also the gap between two notes in music.
Parts of a book.Libretto: Italian for "little book", it's the text of an opera. It sounds right but isn't part of a book.
Parts of a book.Curtain call: The bows taken at the end of a performance, a theatrical ritual, and no part of a printed book.
Parts of a book.Chorus: In Greek drama, a group commenting on the action, and now also the repeated part of a song.
Parts of a book.Bridge: A contrasting section in a song, usually between choruses, and not a component of a printed book.
Parts of a book.Tempo: The speed of a piece of music, often shown in beats per minute, and not a part of any book.
Parts of a book.Crescendo: A gradual rise in loudness in music, from Italian for "growing", and not a part of a book.

Soft things.Pillow: The earliest known pillows were carved from stone, used in ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt to keep the head off the ground.
Soft things.Feather: Down, the fluffy layer beneath a bird's outer feathers, traps so much air that it insulates better than almost anything of its weight.
Soft things.Cotton ball: Cotton fibers are nearly pure cellulose, which is why a cotton ball can soak up many times its own weight in water.
Soft things.Marshmallow: Marshmallows were originally made from the sap of the marsh mallow plant, whose root was a remedy in ancient Egypt and Greece.
Soft things.Teddy bear: The teddy bear is named for Theodore Roosevelt, who in 1902 refused to shoot a bear that hunting guides had tied up.
Soft things.Duvet: Duvet is French for down; in much of Europe a duvet is the standard bedding, while Americans often say comforter.
Soft things.Velvet: Velvet gets its softness from a dense cut pile of upright fibers, and woven silk velvet was once costly enough to be a royal fabric.
Soft things.Fleece blanket: Polar fleece appeared in 1979 and is typically polyester, often spun partly from recycled plastic bottles.
Soft things.Cashmere sweater: Cashmere comes from the fine undercoat of cashmere goats, which is combed out rather than sheared, so each sweater takes several goats' worth.
Soft things.Bunny: A rabbit's teeth never stop growing, which is why bunnies chew constantly to keep them worn down.
Soft things.Mashed potatoes: Potatoes were the first vegetable grown in space, in 1995 aboard the Space Shuttle Columbia.
Soft things.Beanbag chair: The Sacco, designed in Italy in 1968, was the first modern beanbag chair, filled with polystyrene beads rather than beans.
Soft things.Rock: Granite is mostly quartz and feldspar, two minerals harder than a steel knife blade, which is why it dulls tools.
Soft things.Brick: Brick is baked clay, and some Roman brick buildings still stand after nearly two thousand years.
Soft things.Diamond: Diamond tops the Mohs hardness scale, yet a sharp blow can shatter it, because hard doesn't mean tough.
Soft things.Anvil: An anvil is forged steel that is deliberately heavy, so the hammer's energy goes into the metal being shaped instead of making the anvil bounce.
Soft things.Bowling ball: A bowling ball has a dense core inside a hard shell, and adult balls are capped at 16 pounds.
Soft things.Skull: The adult human skull has 22 bones, and all but the jaw are locked together by fixed joints called sutures.
Soft things.Coconut: A coconut is hard on the outside but soft and watery within, and falling ones are a genuine beach hazard.
Soft things.Walnut shell: Crushed walnut shells are used as a mild abrasive for sandblasting and cleaning, which tells you how hard they are.
Soft things.Hammer: A hammer head is hardened steel, and the claw for pulling nails goes back to Roman times.
Soft things.Steel pipe: Steel is iron plus a small amount of carbon, and that bit of carbon is what makes it so hard.
Soft things.Tooth: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body, yet once it's lost the body can't regrow it.
Soft things.Jawbreaker: Jawbreakers are candy, yet rock hard: they're built layer by layer from sugar syrup in a spinning pan, over many days.

Things good at soaking up water.Sponge: Roman toilets had a shared sponge on a stick, called a tersorium, which is a fact best left unthought.
Things good at soaking up water.Paper towel: Paper towels were first sold in 1907, and their quilted texture traps water in tiny pockets.
Things good at soaking up water.Bath towel: A towel's looped terry pile gives water far more surface to cling to than flat fabric.
Things good at soaking up water.Diaper: Disposable diapers contain sodium polyacrylate, a polymer that can absorb hundreds of times its weight in liquid.
Things good at soaking up water.Mop: A mop works by capillary action, water climbing between the fibers.
Things good at soaking up water.Cotton ball: Cotton can absorb many times its own weight in water.
Things good at soaking up water.Kitty litter: Clay kitty litter was invented in 1947 by Ed Lowe, who sold fuller's earth to a neighbor.
Things good at soaking up water.Napkin: Napkin comes from the Old French nappe, meaning tablecloth.
Things good at soaking up water.Chamois: A chamois was originally leather from a mountain goat-antelope, though modern ones are often sheepskin tanned with fish oil.
Things good at soaking up water.Washcloth: A washcloth's flat terry weave grabs and releases water well, and it grows bacteria if left damp.
Things good at soaking up water.Sawdust: Sawdust was once spread on tavern floors to soak up spilled beer.
Things good at soaking up water.Blotting paper: Before ballpoint pens, blotting paper dried ink on letters by soaking it up.
Things good at soaking up water.Raincoat: A raincoat's coating blocks water, the opposite of absorbent, which is why sweat can condense inside it.
Things good at soaking up water.Umbrella: Umbrella fabric is tightly woven nylon treated to repel water, so rain beads up and rolls off.
Things good at soaking up water.Wax paper: Wax paper is coated in wax on both sides to repel liquid, and it isn't oven safe.
Things good at soaking up water.Plastic wrap: Plastic wrap, Saran, was discovered by accident at Dow in 1933 and first used on military equipment.
Things good at soaking up water.Glass: Glass is nonporous and absorbs nothing, though a thin film of water clings to its surface and fogs it.
Things good at soaking up water.Rubber boot: Indigenous Amazonians made rubber footwear long before Europeans arrived, dipping feet in latex.
Things good at soaking up water.Aluminum foil: Aluminum foil's shiny and dull sides perform the same, so it doesn't matter which faces the food.
Things good at soaking up water.Duck feather: Ducks preen oil from a gland near the tail over their feathers, which keeps water off.
Things good at soaking up water.Tarp: Tarps are sheets of coated fabric made specifically to shed rain.
Things good at soaking up water.Teflon pan: Teflon repels both water and oil, and it was discovered by accident in 1938.
Things good at soaking up water.Marble: Marble is dense but not waterproof; it's calcium carbonate, so acid etches it and liquids can stain it.
Things good at soaking up water.Vinyl tablecloth: Vinyl tablecloths wipe clean because spills sit on top instead of soaking in.

Animals with eight legs.Spider: Spiders are arachnids with eight legs, and most can spin silk, which they make in glands and spin out through spinnerets.
Animals with eight legs.Scorpion: Scorpions have eight legs plus pincers, and some species glow blue-green under ultraviolet light because of compounds in their exoskeleton.
Animals with eight legs.Tick: Ticks are arachnids that feed on blood, and the same eight legs help them cling to grass and climb onto passing animals.
Animals with eight legs.Dust mite: A dust mite has eight legs but is under half a millimeter long, so you can't see it, and bedding is its favorite home.
Animals with eight legs.Tarantula: Tarantulas are big hairy spiders, and some can flick irritating hairs from their abdomens as a defense, and they can live for 20 years or more.
Animals with eight legs.Black widow: The black widow's red hourglass is a warning, and its venom is potent, but bites are rarely fatal for healthy adults.
Animals with eight legs.Daddy longlegs: The name is used for harvestmen and cellar spiders, and harvestmen are not true spiders, as they have one oval body part and cannot make silk.
Animals with eight legs.Jumping spider: Jumping spiders have remarkable vision with eight eyes, and they can leap many times their body length, and some can see in color.
Animals with eight legs.Wolf spider: Wolf spiders do not spin webs to catch prey, but chase it, and mothers carry their babies on their backs.
Animals with eight legs.Ant: Ants are insects with six legs, so they miss here, and the body is divided into head, thorax and abdomen.
Animals with eight legs.Bee: Bees have six legs and four wings, and the pollen baskets on their back legs carry pollen home.
Animals with eight legs.Beetle: Beetles are insects, so they have six legs, and their front wings are hard cases that protect the flight wings.
Animals with eight legs.Crab: Crabs have ten legs, including their claws, and they walk sideways because their joints bend that way.
Animals with eight legs.Lobster: Lobsters have ten legs, with the front pair carrying claws, and they were once so plentiful they were fed to prisoners.
Animals with eight legs.Centipede: Centipedes have many more than eight legs, with at least 30 and some species over 100, but they're not arachnids.
Animals with eight legs.Millipede: Millipedes have hundreds of legs, as with each body segment two pairs, so they are not eight-legged.
Animals with eight legs.Grasshopper: A grasshopper is an insect with six legs, and its huge back legs power its jumps.
Animals with eight legs.Squid: A squid has eight arms and two longer tentacles for catching prey, so it has ten limbs in total.
Animals with eight legs.Starfish: Starfish have arms, usually five, and hundreds of tube feet, but no eight legs.
Animals with eight legs.Ladybug: A ladybug is a beetle with six legs, and a single one may eat over 5,000 aphids in its lifetime.
Animals with eight legs.Shrimp: A shrimp has ten legs, five pairs, and a body made for swimming, with its tail fan to dart backward.
Animals with eight legs.Mosquito: A mosquito has six legs, and is just a thin insect, with its long mouthparts, called a proboscis, making it look more spidery.
Animals with eight legs.Butterfly: Butterflies have six legs, and as adults the front pair is small and tucked up in some species.
Animals with eight legs.Cockroach: A cockroach is an insect with six legs, and it can run at about 5 kilometers an hour, fast for its size.

Things that can change color.Chameleon: Chameleons mostly change color to communicate and regulate temperature, by shifting nanocrystals in their skin.
Things that can change color.Octopus: Octopuses change color using thousands of pigment sacs called chromatophores, even though they may be colorblind.
Things that can change color.Mood ring: Mood rings contain heat-sensitive liquid crystals that respond to finger temperature, not true emotions; the fad began in 1975.
Things that can change color.Autumn leaves: Autumn leaves turn when green chlorophyll breaks down, revealing yellow and orange pigments that were there all summer.
Things that can change color.Litmus paper: Litmus is made from lichens and turns red in acid and blue in base.
Things that can change color.Ripening banana: Bananas turn from green to yellow as chlorophyll breaks down, helped along by ethylene gas.
Things that can change color.Cuttlefish: Cuttlefish can ripple waves of color across their skin to mesmerize prey before striking.
Things that can change color.Traffic light: The first traffic light, in London in 1868, used gas lamps, and it reportedly exploded and injured a policeman.
Things that can change color.Arctic fox: Arctic foxes grow a brown summer coat that turns white in winter, matching the snow.
Things that can change color.Hydrangea: Hydrangea flowers turn blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil, thanks to aluminum availability.
Things that can change color.Squid: Squid use chromatophores to flash patterns in seconds, and some deep-sea species glow with bioluminescence.
Things that can change color.Snowshoe hare: Snowshoe hares molt to white for winter, but as snow melts earlier, many stand out against bare ground.
Things that can change color.Zebra: A zebra's stripes are fixed for life, and they likely help deter biting flies.
Things that can change color.Ruby: A ruby is corundum colored red by traces of chromium, and its color is permanent.
Things that can change color.Brick: A brick's red color comes from iron in the clay, and it stays the same for centuries.
Things that can change color.Penguin: A penguin's black and white plumage doesn't change; the pattern helps hide it from predators above and below.
Things that can change color.Crow: Crows are always black, but they can recognize individual human faces and remember them for years.
Things that can change color.Gold bar: Gold doesn't tarnish, so a gold bar keeps its color forever.
Things that can change color.Coal: Coal is black because it's mostly carbon, and its color doesn't change.
Things that can change color.Giant panda: A giant panda's black and white coat is permanent, helping it blend into snow and shade.
Things that can change color.Pearl: A pearl's color is set by the oyster species and doesn't change, though acid or dryness can dull it.
Things that can change color.Elephant: Elephants look gray, but often wear mud and dust that makes them look reddish; their skin doesn't change.
Things that can change color.Granite: Granite's speckled color comes from locked-in minerals, and it never shifts on its own.
Things that can change color.Concrete: Concrete may stain or weather, but it doesn't actively change color.

Found on the outside of a house.Roof: Thatched roofs can last 40 years or more when well kept, and some roofing slate has survived on buildings for over a century.
Found on the outside of a house.Chimney: Tall chimneys draw smoke because hot air rises; in Victorian London, young boys were sent up narrow flues until a law banned the practice.
Found on the outside of a house.Gutter: Rain gutters protect foundations by channeling water away, and a single inch of rain on a 1,000-square-foot roof sheds over 600 gallons.
Found on the outside of a house.Porch: The word comes from Latin porticus, meaning a covered walkway, and the same root gave us the word portico.
Found on the outside of a house.Doorbell: Early doorbells were mechanical pull-wires; the electric version arrived in the 1800s, and video doorbells now record visitors.
Found on the outside of a house.Shutters: Before they were decorative, shutters protected glass from storms and burglars; hurricane shutters still do the same job today.
Found on the outside of a house.Drainpipe: Cast-iron downpipes became common in Victorian houses, and some still carry decorative hopper heads that show the year they were installed.
Found on the outside of a house.Driveway: The name comes from carriage drives, when estate paths were laid out for horse-drawn carriages to sweep up to the front door.
Found on the outside of a house.Weathervane: A weathervane points into the wind, not where it blows to; rooster-topped ones are so common that they are often called weathercocks.
Found on the outside of a house.Doormat: Doormats remove dirt from shoes and cut down on cleaning, and coconut fiber, called coir, is one of the oldest materials used for them.
Found on the outside of a house.Satellite dish: Dishes are curved so signals from satellites about 22,000 miles up are focused onto a single small receiver, the LNB, on the arm.
Found on the outside of a house.Banister: The word is a corruption of baluster, the vertical post; it belongs to indoor staircases, not the outside of a house.
Found on the outside of a house.Pantry: The word comes from Latin panis, bread, because it was originally the room where bread was kept; it sits inside the house.
Found on the outside of a house.Attic: The word comes from Attica, the Greek region, because of an architectural style with a low storey above the cornice; it's a room inside.
Found on the outside of a house.Ceiling: Cathedral ceilings and ornate plaster ones have long been showpieces, but any ceiling is an interior surface, not part of the outside.
Found on the outside of a house.Carpet: Wall-to-wall carpet is an indoor floor covering; it only goes outdoors as artificial turf, and a typical carpet hides dust mites by the million.
Found on the outside of a house.Wardrobe: The word means a room for guarding garments, and a wardrobe is furniture found indoors, so it's never on a house's exterior.
Found on the outside of a house.Fireplace: The hearth is inside, even though its chimney is outside; before central heating, one fireplace often heated the whole house.
Found on the outside of a house.Skirting board: Called baseboard in North America, it hides the join between wall and floor and protects plaster from mops and shoes, indoors only.
Found on the outside of a house.Light switch: The rocker switch is inside by the door; the outdoor equivalent is usually a motion sensor, which makes interior switches not exterior features.
Found on the outside of a house.Wallpaper: Chinese paper hangings reached Europe by the 1500s, and Victorian wallpaper sometimes contained arsenic; it only decorates interior walls.
Found on the outside of a house.Bathtub: Bathtubs sit inside a house; the freestanding clawfoot tub became fashionable in the Victorian era.
Found on the outside of a house.Kitchen sink: The phrase 'everything but the kitchen sink' means nearly everything, and a sink is firmly indoors despite any garden tap.
Found on the outside of a house.Hallway: Hallways are interior corridors; the entrance hall is where a house's front door opens, but it's not found outside.

Landmarks in Washington DC.Lincoln Memorial: Its 36 columns represent the states of the Union at Lincoln's death, and the seated statue is carved from 28 blocks of Georgia white marble.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Washington Monument: At about 555 feet it was the world's tallest structure when finished in 1884; a visible color change marks a pause in construction during the Civil War era.
Landmarks in Washington DC.White House: Its sandstone was painted white to protect it from weather, and the building has been the president's residence since John Adams moved in in 1800.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Capitol: Its cast-iron dome, finished during the Civil War, weighs millions of pounds, and Lincoln insisted work continue as a sign the Union would endure.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Smithsonian: Founded with a bequest from British scientist James Smithson, who never visited the US, it is now the world's largest museum complex.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Jefferson Memorial: The domed memorial overlooks the Tidal Basin, where thousands of cherry trees given by Japan in 1912 bloom each spring.
Landmarks in Washington DC.National Mall: This long green park stretches about two miles between the Capitol and the Lincoln Memorial and has hosted huge marches and inaugurations.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Library of Congress: With well over 170 million items, it is the largest library in the world, and it grew from Thomas Jefferson's personal book collection.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Kennedy Center: The performing arts center was named in memory of President John F. Kennedy, and it hosts the annual Kennedy Center Honors.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Supreme Court: The justices met in the Capitol for decades; their marble building across the street, with the words 'Equal Justice Under Law', opened in 1935.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Liberty Bell: The cracked bell lives in Philadelphia, not Washington; it became a symbol of freedom partly through abolitionists in the 1800s.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Statue of Liberty: Built in France and shipped across the Atlantic in 350 pieces, she stands in New York Harbor, nowhere near the capital.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Gateway Arch: At 630 feet it's the tallest man-made monument in the US, and it stands in St. Louis, Missouri, marking westward expansion.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Mount Rushmore: Sculpted in South Dakota's Black Hills between 1927 and 1941, it shows four presidents, each face about 60 feet tall.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Space Needle: Built for the 1962 World's Fair, this Seattle tower was designed in a few weeks from a sketch on a napkin, as the legend goes.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Golden Gate Bridge: Its famous color, International Orange, helps it stand out in San Francisco's fog, and its towers rise about 750 feet above the water.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Alamo: This former Spanish mission in San Antonio, Texas, was the site of a famous 1836 siege where defenders held out for 13 days.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Graceland: Elvis Presley's Memphis mansion draws about half a million visitors a year, making it one of the most visited homes in America.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Pentagon: It's in Arlington, Virginia, not DC proper, and it's one of the world's largest office buildings with about 17 miles of corridors.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Arlington Cemetery: It is across the Potomac in Virginia, on land once owned by Robert E. Lee's family, and is the burial place of Kennedy and the Tomb of the Unknowns.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Mount Vernon: George Washington's estate sits in Virginia, about 15 miles south of the city, and he designed much of its grounds himself.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Hoover Dam: On the Nevada-Arizona border, this 1936 dam holds back Lake Mead and was once the world's largest concrete structure.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Independence Hall: The Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution were both debated here in Philadelphia, not in the capital.
Landmarks in Washington DC.Fenway Park: Boston's Red Sox ballpark opened in 1912 and is the oldest in Major League Baseball, famous for its tall left-field wall, the Green Monster.

Animals that give us textile fibres.Sheep: Sheep supply wool, and merino sheep produce fibers so fine they feel soft enough to wear next to the skin.
Animals that give us textile fibres.Alpaca: Alpaca fiber is warm, silky and has no lanolin, so it's usually less itchy than sheep wool.
Animals that give us textile fibres.Llama: Llamas are mainly pack animals, but their coarser fleece is spun into rugs and ropes in the Andes.
Animals that give us textile fibres.Goat: Cashmere comes from the undercoat of cashmere goats, and mohair comes from Angora goats; both are luxury fibers.
Animals that give us textile fibres.Rabbit: Angora wool comes from Angora rabbits, which are sheared or plucked; it's very light and fluffy.
Animals that give us textile fibres.Camel: Camel hair is warm and light, and is used in coats; the soft fibers come from the animal's undercoat shed each spring.
Animals that give us textile fibres.Yak: Yaks give a soft down fiber called khullu, used in Tibet and Mongolia for clothing and tents.
Animals that give us textile fibres.Musk ox: Musk ox wool is called qiviut, a very warm Arctic fiber, many times warmer than sheep wool, and collected as the animal molts.
Animals that give us textile fibres.Vicuña: The vicuña is a wild Andean relative of the llama, and its wool is among the world's rarest and costliest.
Animals that give us textile fibres.Silkworm: Silkworms are the caterpillars of the Bombyx mori moth; each cocoon is a single thread, roughly a kilometer long.
Animals that give us textile fibres.Pig: Pigs aren't harvested for textiles, though pig bristles go into brushes and the leather is used for gloves.
Animals that give us textile fibres.Chicken: Chicken feathers are used for stuffing and bedding, but they aren't spun into textile fibers.
Animals that give us textile fibres.Kangaroo: Kangaroo hide makes strong, thin leather, but it isn't a fiber, so it doesn't count as textile fiber.
Animals that give us textile fibres.Zebra: Zebras are hunted for stripes by some, but no one spins zebra hair into fabric.

Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Adenine: One of four DNA bases, it pairs with thymine. It is also part of ATP, the molecule cells use as energy currency.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Thymine: It is found in DNA but not RNA, where uracil takes its place. It pairs with adenine through two hydrogen bonds.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Guanine: It pairs with cytosine, and the name comes from guano, since it was first isolated from bird droppings in 1844.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Cytosine: It pairs with guanine through three bonds, making G-C pairs stronger than A-T pairs.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Double helix: Watson and Crick described this twisted-ladder shape in 1953, helped by Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Nucleotide: A single DNA unit made of a sugar, a phosphate and a base. A human genome has about 3 billion base pairs.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Deoxyribose: The sugar in DNA. 'Deoxy' means it lacks one oxygen atom compared with ribose, and that makes DNA more stable than RNA.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Phosphate group: Phosphates link with sugars to form the backbone of each DNA strand, giving DNA its negative charge.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Base pair: Two bases joined across the helix, A with T or G with C, and it is also the unit used to measure DNA length.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Hydrogen bonds: Weak bonds hold the two strands together, which lets enzymes unzip DNA when cells copy it.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Chromosome: A long coiled DNA molecule packed with proteins. Humans have 23 pairs, and stretched out, the DNA in one cell is about two metres long.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Uracil: It replaces thymine in RNA, so it is not a DNA building block. It pairs with adenine.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Ribose: The sugar of RNA, with one more oxygen atom than DNA's deoxyribose, which makes RNA less stable.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Amino acid: These are the units of proteins, not DNA. Cells use 20 standard types, and DNA's code tells them which to link.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Ribosome: This cellular machine reads RNA to build proteins. It is made of RNA and protein itself, not DNA.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Anticodon: It is a three-base stretch on transfer RNA that matches the codon on messenger RNA when protein is made.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Mitochondria: Cell power plants. They do carry a small loop of their own DNA, but they are organelles, not DNA's building blocks.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Peptide: A short chain of amino acids. Link enough of them and you get a protein, which is outside DNA.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Enzyme: A protein that speeds up reactions, like DNA polymerase which copies DNA. It acts on DNA but is not part of it.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Protein: Made from amino acids, not from DNA's units. DNA contains the instructions that tell cells how to build them.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Glucose: A sugar that cells burn for energy. It is not part of DNA, which uses deoxyribose.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Lipid: Fats and oils that build cell membranes, which have nothing to do with the structure of DNA.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Cellulose: A sugar polymer making up plant cell walls, and the most abundant organic compound on Earth. It is not part of DNA.
Building blocks of DNA (not RNA or prote.Ribozyme: An RNA molecule that can act as an enzyme, which supports the idea that early life ran on RNA.
